text: Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Last night I spoke to President Zelenskyy to discuss progress that President Trump had made with Russia towards a ceasefire, and I took the opportunity to reaffirm our unwavering support to the people of Ukraine. Mr. Speaker, I'm deeply concerned about the resumption of Israeli military action in Gaza. The images of parents carrying their children, young children to hospitals that have emerged over the last few days are truly shocking, alongside the sheer number of people who've been killed. And we will do all that we can to ensure the resumption of the ceasefire to get the remaining hostages out and to get aid that's desperately needed in. Mr. Speaker, the whole house will want to celebrate the extraordinary life of Group Captain John Paddy Hemingway, the last known pilot of the Battle of Britain. The courage of his generation, the fearlessness, sense of duty and service, secured our freedom and we will never forget them. Mr. Speaker, this morning I had meetings with ministerial colleagues and others, in addition to my duties in this house, I shall have further such meetings later today.

Can I thank him for doing what he was asked to do, which is raising this case here. The loss of a child is simply unbearable, and I think most of us, including myself, simply wouldn't know how we would be able to react. And I think the whole house will want to send its deepest condolences to Laura and to all of Taylor's family and friends. I will happily make sure that the meeting that he requests takes place so we can reassure that we are committed to supporting life-saving and life-improving research and doing all we can to improve how we prevent, detect, manage, and treat cancer. Thank you.

Well, I think he's a superb job for Peterborough and we're proud that our employment rights bill is tackling the cost of insecure work and we're delivering that pay rise for 3 million of the lowest paid. We know the leader of the opposition opposes all that. She thinks the minimum wage is a burden and the maternity pay is excessive. It's the same old Tories. They oppose the minimum wage in the first place. They've learned absolutely nothing.

Mr. Speaker, we have delivered record investment into this country. Three interest rates cut in a row and wages are going up faster than prices, which is a massive cost of living boost. That's after only eight months, after 14 years of absolute failure. What did they leave? Interest rates 11%, massive 22 black hole million black hole in the economy. They crashed the economy. We're rebuilding Britain.

Mr. Speaker, the OBR will present their numbers, there'll be a spring statement next week. But Mr. Speaker, she still hasn't we've got record investment into this country, interest rates have been cut and she talks about she talks about national insurance. We had to fill the 22 billion black hole that they left. We've invested in the NHS, in schools and public services. We're pressing on with planning, with infrastructure and regulation. But I understand the leader of the opposition is straight talking, so perhaps she can help us with this. Is she going to reverse the NICs increase? If not, what's the point? If so, what other taxes is she raising to fill the hole? One way or the other.

I noticed she didn't say they're going to reverse the National Insurance rises. That's exactly what it is. She wants all the benefits, but they can't say how they're going to pay for them. She carps from the sidelines but can't make her mind up whether she supports or doesn't support national insurance rises. We've made provision for hospices, we've made provisions for charities, but we had to secure the economy, we had to fill the 22 billion pound black hole that they disgracefully left.

Mr. Speaker, we've already invested 100 million pounds for adult and children's hospices and additional 26 million pounds in funding through the children's hospices grant. But we can't get away what we were doing in that budget, the root cause, which was fixing the economy they left so badly damaged. A 22 billion pound black hole. Perhaps she'll start the next question with an apology.

Mr. Speaker, I've already set out the position in relation to hospices. She says that she wants to swap sides. I mean, heaven forbid. After 14 years of breaking everything, we're getting on with the job of fixing it and all she can do is carp from the sidelines without absolutely no policy.

Mr. Speaker, she's got such prescriptive questions she can't actually adapt them to the answers that I'm giving. I mean, Mr. Speaker, I think she now calls herself a conservative realist. Well, I'm realistic about the conservatives. The reality is they left open borders and she was the cheerleader. They crashed the economy, mortgages went through the roof, the NHS was left on its knees, and they hollowed out the armed forces. This government's already delivered two million extra NHS appointments, 750 breakfast clubs, record returns of people who shouldn't be here, and a fully funded increase in our defense spending. That is the difference that a Labor government makes.

Mr. Speaker, I have lived with the impact of disability in our family through my mother and brother all my life. I do understand the human impact of this. But the current system is morally and economically indefensible, and we're right to reform it. And nobody should be defending the broken status quo. We are proceeding on three principles: that if you can work, you should work. If you need help into work, the state should help you, not hinder you. And if you can never work, you must be supported and protected. They are the right principles, but we can't leave the current system as it is.

Can I start by pointing out that because of the changes we made at that budget, we were able to put record amounts of money into our National Health Service and vitally important that we did so. And it isn't right to simply oppose the measures we had to take to raise the money and at the same time say, as the honorable gentleman does, that he wants the benefits of the increase in funding to the NHS. The two can't sit together. We have already invested an additional 3.7 billion pounds of funding into social care, including 880 million to increase the social care grant. So we are taking steps, but the basic point remains, which is we can't make the investment into the NHS if we don't raise the money. And you can't simply oppose any raising of money and at the same time welcome the money into the NHS.

Well, I'm grateful to him for raising this important issue and it is a matter of deep concern. We've already developing a rural crime strategy, but we'll happily work with him and others to develop it further.

Can I join him in commending the West Midlands Police for keeping his community safe. We are doubling our investment to 200 million pounds towards the recruitment of 13,000 neighborhood police, giving every community a named officer to help tackle violent crime. And we're currently working through bids with forces to ensure that we do so, and I'll make sure he gets a meeting with the relevant policing minister to discuss.

Mr. Speaker, we do have a proportional tax system and we have raised tax on the wealthiest under this government. But her advice would count for a bit more if their manifesto hadn't been a recipe for 80 billion pounds of extra borrowing. That is to do exactly what Liz Truss did to the economy and that doesn't help any of the people that she's claiming to support.

Well, he's very right to raise this important project, which we are working for. And it's vital that we do unleash the potential of the Oxford-Cambridge Corridor and of course, Bedford by generating growth jobs and opportunity. And we're doing that by speeding up the delivery of new infrastructure projects, slashing red tape, and getting Britain building.

Well, he's right, too many people with eating disorders are not getting the treatment that they need. The NHS is expanding eating disorder treatment services with a focus on accessing treatment earlier and closer to home. And we're also providing access to specialist mental health professionals in every school, and I'll make sure he's kept up to date.

Mr. Speaker, it's totally unacceptable for anyone to feel intimidated or unsafe due to the actions of reckless and selfish individuals. Whatever the vehicle, our bill gives police forces stronger powers to seize them immediately and put a stop to anti-social behavior. That's our plan for change in action, making our streets and communities safer.

No, what it says in my favor is they had 14 years, including five with a majority of 80. They didn't need to consult, get on with it. They had a majority of 80 for the last five years. They're now carping on with some of their ideas. 14 years and they didn't implement a single one. They simply broke the system. They're in no place to lecture other people.

Well, the situation he describes is an appalling indictment of the SNP record. The party opposite left record homelessness in England. The SNP record is equally shameful. A record number of children in temporary accommodation. Mr. Speaker, we're investing one billion pounds to tackle homelessness, we're abolishing no-fault evictions and building 1.5 million new homes. Meanwhile, the SNP have cut their affordable housing budget. They've had the largest settlement since devolution, they've got the power and the money, now it's time they started delivering.
Mr. Speaker, we are rolling out 350 banking hubs across all communities and I'll happily arrange for her to have a meeting with the minister to discuss how that might affect her constituency.

Well, Mr. Speaker, Petroineos have said that every employee made redundant will get 18 months' full pay. The Project Willow report that's come out today says how we can support a sustainable industrial future for Grangemouth, which is incredibly important, delivering jobs and economic growth. As he references, I've announced 200 million pounds through the National Wealth Fund to secure the site's long-term future. And of course, that's backed by the 100 million pound Falkirk and Grangemouth growth deal and the training guarantee to support workers into good jobs. They're all the actions that we were taking on this very, very important issue.

Well, the victims of this scandal have suffered unspeakably, and I'm pleased that at the budget, we set aside the 11.8 billion pounds to compensate them in relation to this appalling scandal. I would gently point out that the party opposite was committed, rightly, to this compensation, but didn't provide a single penny in the column to pay for it. The Infected Blood Compensation Authority has been established and began to make payments last year. Over a billion in interim payments have been made, and we do remain completely committed to cooperating with the inquiry and acting on its recommendations.

Yes, and at home we are watching Adolescent with our children. I've got a 16-year-old boy and a 14-year-old girl. It's a very, very good documentary to watch or drama. This violence carried out by young men influenced by what they see online is a real problem. It's abhorrent, and we have to tackle it. We are putting in specialist rape and sexual offenses teams in every police force doing work on the 999 calls. But this is also a matter of culture that I think it's important that across the whole house, we tackle this emerging and growing problem.

Well, we are working closely with our European colleagues and the EU in particular, and we are working to a reset of the relationship. We won't be returning to freedom of movement. I've made that repeatedly clear, but we're making good progress.

She's right, further education plays a critical role in giving young people the skills and confidence that they need and of course the training we need for the future. We are investing 400 million pounds on education for 16 to 19-year-olds this year, and our levy-funded growth and skills offer will create jobs in key industries. And I can assure her that the funding will deliver enough places for young people.

Yes, but they did leave a bit of a mess that we are clearing up, having hollowed out our armed forces and having not made the necessary investment that we needed in our defense. We've announced the largest sustained increase since the Cold War of 2.5% by 2027 and 3% in the next parliament, subject to economic circumstances. So yes, we are getting on with the job and clearing up the mess that they left.

Well, she's right, remediation has been far too slow and everybody deserves a safe and secure home. We've signed a contract with 54 major developers who will pay for or fix over 1,700 buildings, and we're accelerating that progress. We will take tough action against those who evade their responsibilities. We will recover taxpayers' funds and make sure those responsible pay up and fix unsafe buildings quickly.

Mr. Speaker, net-zero is of course not easy, but it's a huge opportunity to boost our growth, our jobs, and our economy. And so he knows my views on that. But, you know, he complains that I have better ideas if they stop falling over Putin. And I understand the member for Clacton wants to be Prime Minister, he can't even lead a party that fits in the back of a taxi.

She's right, everybody needs to be able to access a home that is suitable for them and meets their needs. The planning rules, Mr. Speaker, already mean councils must consider the needs of disabled people when planning new homes. And we will go further, setting out our policies on accessible new homes very shortly. And we're boosting the disabled facilities grant by 172 million pounds, helping more people make vital improvements and live independent lives.

Well, on both points. I spoke to President Zelenskyy last night following the discussions yesterday to discuss the way forward. On the wider question of the assets, look, it's complicated, but we're working with others to see what is possible. But it isn't straightforward.

Well, I'm very grateful for him for raising Grangemouth again for the second time in this session, and that's because it's centrally important. He'll have heard what I had to say about the projects that we're looking at to ensure the long-term future of Grangemouth, the interim measures that are being taken, and of course, the 200 million pounds of the Wealth Fund that I announced just a few weeks ago.

Well, I thank him for raising this and he's right to do so. It's a shocking issue, and the case he refers to is a truly shocking case. I think that's agreed across the house. We are working on this and I'll make sure that he gets an update to ensure that he's across the detail of what we're doing. Final question.

She is a passionate advocate and has been for a long time on this issue and I pay tribute to that. But as she rightly acknowledges, the current system is broken. And this is where I disagree with her. I think one in eight young people not in employment, training or education, that's a million young people. I think that's a moral issue, Mr. Speaker. Because all the evidence suggests that someone in that situation at that stage of their life is going to find it incredibly difficult ever to get out of that level of dependence. That cuts across the opportunity and aspiration at the root of my values and Labor values about how we take working people forward. So I do see it as a moral issue. I'm not going to turn away from that. I am genuinely shocked that a million people young people in that position and I'm not prepared to shrug my shoulders and walk past it. That completes Prime Minister's Questions.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Today's spring statement will showcase a government going further and faster on the economy. Greenlighting the lower Thames crossing, investing 2 billion pounds for 80,000 affordable homes for working families, 60,000 young people being trained as the next generation of construction workers, and fixing millions of potholes. We are undoing a decade of stagnation, driving jobs and opportunities for working people, and securing Britain's future. Mr. Speaker, tomorrow I'll meet President Macron in Paris to discuss further our efforts to secure a lasting peace in Ukraine. And may I welcome the delegation from Bring Back Kids initiative to the gallery. The abduction of Ukrainian children is grotesque. And the UK will play our full part to bring them home. It's a stark reminder that any peace settlement must see Russia held accountable for their deplorable actions. Mr. Speaker, this morning I had meetings with ministerial colleagues and others. In addition to my duties in this house, I shall have further such meetings later today.

Mr. Speaker, our plan for change already cut NHS waiting lists by almost 200,000. That's five months in a row during the winter months. The local trust waiting lists in his area are down 93 percent and he's doing a great job for his community. We've already delivered 2 million extra appointments that we promised because of the record investment in the budget. And the party opposite can't have it both ways. If they welcome NHS investment, they can't criticize raising the money to pay for it.

Because it's completely unnecessary. I've got two teenage children. Almost every school bans phones in school. They do it already. We need to concentrate on what's really important here, which is getting to the content that children shouldn't be accessing. That's where I would genuinely like to work across the House because I think there's a huge amount of work to do. But the battle is not with schools that already ban phones in school. The battle, and this is an important emerging battle, is to work together to ensure that we can ensure that the content that children are accessing wherever they are is suitable for their age.

We need to ensure that all schools do this, but the vast majority do. Look, it is really important that we focus on the battle we have to have with mobile phones, which is the content that children are able to access. And we need to ensure that that is controlled wherever they are. So it's a question of having the right battle on the right issue, not wasting time on something where almost all schools are already banning mobile phones.

Mr. Speaker, she talks about the record of the last government. Under their watch, a third of children started school without appropriate level development. And that is not being able to use a knife and fork. A quarter left primary school without the required standard of reading, writing, and maths. And one in five was regularly absent. That's why we're pushing up standards, more information from Ofsted, transparency for parents, more interventions where schools need it.

Mr. Speaker, it was Labour that introduced academies. We pushed up standards and this is not ideological. I'm a parent of two teenage children, both of whom go to a state school. So I'm vested in this and it matters hugely to me. Nothing ideological about it. That is where we're driving up standards as we always have done.

Mr. Speaker, this government at the budget put a record amount into our schools, just as we put a record amount into our NHS and into our public services who were utterly failed under the last government. But yet again, yet again, she wants all the benefits, the NHS, but she can't say how she's going to pay for it. That's what got us into the mess in the first place.

Yes, take the example of schools going into academies. The vast majority of schools are already academies. Therefore, we need to think again about what we do about failing schools that are already academies. We need to go on to the next chapter. And this, they never take the big decisions. And that's why we ended up with their record. Open borders, which she was the cheerleader for. A crashed economy, mortgages through the roof. The NHS on its knees. Hollowed out armed forces. And what have we got already under this government? 2 million extra NHS appointments. 750 breakfast clubs, including one in her constituency. Record numbers of people being returned who shouldn't be here. And a fully funded increase in defense spending. That's the difference a Labour government makes.

He's a great champion for his constituency. We are investing 600 million pounds to train up to 60,000 more skilled housebuilders so we can support the next generation and deliver 1.5 million new homes. We're creating Tech Excellence colleges and investing in Stansted Airport, creating 5,000 jobs nearby, which will create more opportunities for young people in Harlow.

Well, yes, of course, as he well knows. On the point he makes about online safety, it is important. There are new measures coming in in the next few months which are very important under the Act. And we need to see whether we can go further on this issue because there are concerns as to whether they go far enough. But will the laws be made in this place? Of course they will.

Mr. Speaker, we work with the United States on a daily basis. And I think the honorable gentleman would like to think of himself as sort of reasonable and when he's not jumping in Windermere, quite serious. But unpicking our relations with the US on defense and security is neither responsible nor serious.

Every person should have the right to work. And we will always protect the most severely disabled and those with lifelong health conditions. For Medina and the 200,000 others like her who can work and want to work, we need to support them. And that's why we're investing 1 billion pounds in personalized tailoring employment programs and introducing the Right to Try work guarantee. The party opposite presided over a failed system that didn't help them and then blamed them. We will never do that.

Well, I'm grateful to him for sharing his personal experience on this and he's right to do so. My family has lived with disability for many years as well, so I do understand the human element of this. We do need to give support to those that need it. We do need to help those who want to work into work. And we need to be clear that those who can work should work. In England we inherited a failed system that couldn't be defended. But it's also failing in Scotland. 84,000 young Scots, he focuses on young people, that's 15 percent of young Scots not in employment, education or training. That is terrible. Almost 300,000 Scots economically inactive due to temporary or long-term illness. Now what we're doing is taking the steps to help people into work, a billion pounds of employment support. They have record funding under the budget. What are they going to do to help the young Scots who are being failed by their government?

Well it is really important that we unleash the economic potential of North Wales, including kickstarting the investment zone, backed by major businesses, Mr. Speaker, like Airbus and JCB to leverage 1 billion pounds of private investment. Investing 975 million pounds to benefit aerospace workers at Broughton, where I met the fantastic young workers there and securing 1 billion pound investment in Shotton Mill, securing 300 jobs on Deeside. And we put a record amount of money into the Welsh government at the budget, a budget decision which was opposed by Plaid.
The right honorable member asks about shale gas. There are very real economic and environmental consequences to fracking. And communities have clearly said no.

He knows there are real consequences of fracking as I've set out. But what we need to do to secure our independence and lower bills for the next generation of jobs is move at speed to renewable energy. And that's why I'm pleased that record investment is coming into renewable energy so that tyrants like Putin can't put his boot on our throat. Now if the party opposite don't want to support that investment, they should say so.

Can I congratulate all colleagues working on this bill and taking part in the debate. It is an important issue on which there are different views across the house and within parties. The bill is a matter for the house, but it is the government's role to ensure every piece of legislation that passes through Parliament is effective and workable. So we'll continue to work with my honorable friend as the bill sponsor to do that. In the same way, Mr. Speaker, we would for every private member's bill which passes second reading. And if parliament chooses to pass this bill, the government will implement it in a way that is safe and practical.

We are investing 100 million pounds for adult and children's hospices to improve facilities, equipment and accommodation as well as 26 million pounds in funding through the children's hospice grant. But their cries and moaning would have a lot more value if they started their questions with an apology for crashing the economy in the first place.

Look, he's right. Potholes are a real nuisance. And if you're using your car for work or your van and you hit a pothole, you're looking at a bill of several hundred pounds, which is unbudgeted for so many working families. That's why we're handing the West Midlands Combined Authority an additional 8.6 million pounds to help repair their roads, part of a record 1.6 billion pounds invested across the country. On top of that, Mr. Speaker, every council must now publish how many potholes they've filled so we can show that we're making progress and that we're delivering something that didn't happen under the last government.

Well I'm grateful for this. This is a really important issue. And Labour in Scotland has been clear that they'd separate this role. That's the right thing to do for the reasons that have just been articulated, the obvious thing to do. And that's obviously what we do in England and Wales. Now there've been calls for review on this since 2021, but the SNP has not acted fast on those reviews. They really do need to bring forward proposals now to deal with the problems that have been sitting there for a very, very long time.

I'm grateful to him for emphasizing this again. Russia's abduction of Ukrainian children is sickening and I think across the House we would all agree on that. A peace settlement in Ukraine must see Russia held to account and the children reunited with their families. And in specific reference to his question, the UK is playing our full part in international efforts including funding the Bring Kids Back initiative through the Partnership Fund for a Resilient Ukraine. And I want to reassure the whole house we'll do everything we can to see these children returned and reintegrated as safely and as quickly as is possible.

Well we will set out details just as soon as we can on the basis of the principles that I set out earlier. The scheme overall in terms of welfare is not defendable on terms, but it must be a scheme that supports those that need it and details will be set out.

I thank him for his question. He does great work to bring our communities together especially in Slough. Look, any form of racial or religious based hatred is abhorrent and has no place in society. We have set aside over 50 million pounds to protect faith communities and freedom of worship. That's the right thing to do. It's a shame that we have to do it. And our 15 million community recovery fund has been supporting communities affected by the disorder last summer. Again the right thing to do, but it's a shame that we have to do it.

Well look, he's right to raise the concern about the situation in Heathrow. I think everybody's very concerned by what happened last week. There are clearly questions that need to be answered on a number of fronts in relation to what happened and an investigation is ongoing. But I'm not going to announce particular parts of our policy and strategy here at this stage.

I thank her for fighting SNP incompetence on behalf of her constituents. Yet again the SNP are failing island communities. Hospital appointments are being missed and livelihoods destroyed. And Scotland has a proud history of shipbuilding and engineering. The SNP should be supporting Scottish workers and focusing on delivering for our communities.

I hope she'll forgive me. The details of the particular incinerator she speaks of I don't know the details. I'm not across that, but I will make sure that she gets an answer to her question in written form as soon as possible.

Well, Mr. Speaker, this is a once-in-a-generation moment for security of our country and our continent. We've set out that fully funded increase in defense spending to 2.5 percent in 2027, the biggest sustained boost since the Cold War. But that must benefit British jobs and British businesses. And that's why I'll make sure that he gets the meeting that he wants with the relevant minister.

He's a superb local champion. And regardless of which club any of us support, they share a love of the game and they are at the heart of our communities. And Albion Rovers is exactly that, a huge point of local pride. And I'd encourage all efforts to secure the future of the club.

Well, could I thank him for raising this issue. The courage of these campaigners after simply appalling cases is astounding and I find it humbling. I'm pleased the Minister for Victims will be meeting the group, I think today, and I look forward to meeting them in the future because we must prioritize victims and make sure sentences punish offenders and protect the public. So thank him for raising this really important set of cases. That completes Prime Minister's Questions. Front bench changeover.

Mr. Speaker, just picking up on your comments, can I say that on Monday night I spoke to President Zelenskyy, and he wanted me to pass on to you his thanks for attending in Ukraine, particularly on the third anniversary of the massacre at Bucha, which I've been to Bucha. It's a terrible third anniversary, so I pass on those thanks. Mr. Speaker, we've been preparing for all eventualities ahead of the confirmation of US tariffs later today. Let me be clear with the House: a trade war is in nobody's interests, and the country deserves, and we will take, a calm, pragmatic approach. That's why constructive talks are progressing to agree a wider economic prosperity deal with the US. That's why we're working with all industries and sectors likely to be impacted. Our decisions will always be guided by our national interest, and that's why we have prepared for all eventualities and we will rule nothing out. Mr. Speaker, our deepest sympathies are with the people of Myanmar and Thailand. We are sending immediate life-saving support to assist their efforts. May I also extend my personal condolences to the family, friends, and colleagues of Christina McKelvie. She was much loved and will be sorely missed, especially by our colleagues in the SNP here and in Scotland. Mr. Speaker, this morning I had meetings with ministerial colleagues and others. In addition to my duties in this House, I shall have further such meetings later today.

Well, he's absolutely right. We can commit to the triple lock because we've restored stability after they crashed the economy. And that means, Mr. Speaker, next week 12 million pensioners will receive up to 470 pounds more. That's an extra 1,900 pounds over this Parliament, including one million pensioners in Scotland. And the contrast couldn't be clearer. The Shadow Chancellor called the triple lock unsustainable, and the Leader of the Opposition wants to means-test the state pension so that she can cut it.

Mr. Speaker, she says the triple lock was Conservative policy. It was once thought to be the party of sound finances, but they blew all of that. Mr. Speaker, she asks what we're doing. We're clearing up the mess that they left. We're dealing with global instability and we recognize the pressures that are bearing down on businesses and individuals and working people. That's why we're rolling up our sleeves and yesterday, Mr. Speaker, I was pleased to announce the national living wage increasing by 1,400 pounds. That's a pay rise for millions of workers. We've announced 150 pounds for the warm homes discount, extended now to six million households. That's one in five families. And wages are going up faster than prices. And never forget: the party opposite, worst living standards on record, inflation up to 11 percent, public services left on their knees.

Well, her fantasy figure is about as much use as Liz Truss's economic planning. And she turns up every week to carp from the sidelines about the decisions we made at the budget. Yesterday, Mr. Speaker, she held a press conference and she couldn't say whether she would reverse the decisions that we made at the budget. Now, I understand, because she can't bring herself to say that she doesn't want the investment of an extra 26 billion pounds in our NHS. I'm not surprised at that. That's two million extra appointments, that's a thousand more GPs, a pay rise for nurses, etc., etc. But let me get her position right, if I can follow it. She wants the extra 26 billion pounds in the NHS, Mr. Speaker, that was paid for by the national insurance rise. She wants that. She doesn't want to reverse the national insurance rises. So she's now reached this absurd position of voting against the budget, carping against the budget, that she actually agrees with.

Well, all I have to ask is if she doesn't want people poorer, why didn't she resign when she was in government? Mr. Speaker, the last government put up council tax for 12 years in a row. She, I think, was actually Minister for Council Tax. And in the year she was in, what did she do? She put it up. And even now, the Conservatives' own Local Government Association manifesto, so currently their position, page 9: 'We ask the government to remove the caps on council tax.' So who's leading the charge? Hampshire County Council, they wanted a 15% hike. We said no. Slough Council wanted a hike. We said no. Windsor and Maidenhead, was Tory now Lib Dem, they wanted a hike and we said no. And it's no surprise that council tax is 300 pounds cheaper under Labour councils than under Tory councils.

I think she must have picked up the script she was using a few weeks ago. Because it was only then she said in the spring statement we're going to put up taxes. But look, Mr. Speaker, in relation to the situation in Birmingham, it is completely unacceptable. I fully support the council in declaring it a major incident to resolve the situation, and we'll put in whatever additional support is needed. But when the party opposite was in government, we lost more days to strike action than in any year since the 1980s. NHS workers were on the picket line, not on the front line, and that sent waiting lists through the roof. So we'll take no lectures on industrial harmony from them.

Mr. Speaker, she must be the only person left in the country who actually thinks they did well on the economy when they were in power. That was what was tested at the last election. They... living standards the worst on record, inflation 11% it soared up to, the NHS on its knees. And Mr. Speaker, she's so obsessed, she's so obsessed with talking down the country that she's not read the OBR forecast properly. Growth up in 2026, '27 up, 2028 up, 2029 up. And thanks to our planning reforms, the largest growth measure the OBR have ever costed. And what did the Tories do when the bill came before Parliament? They abstained. Well, you don't grow the economy or build houses by abstaining. They're the same old party, they haven't changed, nothing's new.

We're taking a calm, pragmatic approach and keeping our feet on the ground. We are... there are constructive talks that are ongoing on a wider economic prosperity deal with the US. That is really important at this moment. We are working with all sectors that are likely to be impacted, and we're guided by our national interest at all times. And that's why we've said we won't rule anything out. But it is important at a moment like this that we don't have knee-jerk reactions, that we are actually cool-headed about this, and that's why we won't rule anything out. But she must be... she was the Trade Secretary, she was the Trade Secretary, Mr. Speaker, who failed, who failed to get a trade deal with the US.

Well, I thank her for raising this. It is an important issue, and there are issues in relation to Northern Ireland in particular that we have to deal with very carefully. We will, Mr. Speaker, always put the national interest first, and that's why I'm pleased that talks are ongoing and they're constructive talks. I do believe that a trade war is in nobody's interest and all of the sectors and industries impacted are of the same view. So we'll continue to make that progress in the national interest.

Mr. Speaker, I think every week he tries to tempt me to make what I think is a false choice between our relationship with the US and our relationship with other countries, particularly Europe. I think that's the wrong choice on defense, on security, intelligence, for reasons that we've rehearsed across this chamber. I also think it's wrong on trade and the economy. We have a good deal of trade, a balanced trade relationship with the US, and I believe that our interests are best served by calmly trying to secure a deal which is in our national interest, whilst at the same time preparing and leaving all options on the table.

Mr. Speaker, in relation to his comments at the beginning of the question, I really do think it's not sensible to say the first response should be to jump into a trade war with the US. That cannot be the first response of the United Kingdom, and I will resist his urgings to do that. In relation to water, he's absolutely right to point out the appalling record on water of the party opposite. Just like your record on everything was appalling, and that's why I'm really pleased that we've passed the Water Act already to take the necessary measures, but we will go further.

I believe it's best for communities when their leaders have skin in the game. Helen Goodwin grew up in Stapleton, went to college in Filton, and has a great record fighting for the community where she's raising her family. Mr. Speaker, our plan for change has delivered record funding for the West of England. That's more money for better buses, for potholes, and getting young people into work. That's the difference a Labour mayor working with a Labour government delivers for the West of England.

Can I thank him for raising this issue, which is of real importance to his constituents and everybody in Northern Ireland? It is a very serious issue. That's why we need to be calm and pragmatic. And I think that's what workers and businesses in Northern Ireland would want to see from this government at a time like this. We are, as he would expect, looking carefully at the details of any retaliatory tariffs announced by the EU, if they are, and what impact they might have on businesses. As he knows, where goods do not enter the EU, then businesses can claim a full reimbursement of any EU duties paid. But I reassure him: the interests of Northern Ireland are at the forefront of our decisions. And he may want to know that this morning, the Business Secretary spoke to the Northern Ireland Executive, because this is a serious issue and we need to work together to resolve it in the interests of everybody in Northern Ireland.

Well, I mean, the party opposite tried an open borders experiment. We are now tackling illegal migration. They talked about flights, Mr. Speaker. We've already removed 24,000 people with no right to be here. Under their Rwanda scheme, which was only ever supposed to return I think 300 people a year. What we've achieved in nine months would have taken them 80 years. We've replaced a gimmick with a real deterrent.

He and I share a love of the Lake District, and we still go back there with our children now. This is a serious issue, obviously, and that's why we've put a record amount into farming at the budget, but also set out our roadmap. But I'll happily make sure that he gets a meeting with the relevant minister to go through that and to take on board any points he has to make in relation to it.

The Deputy Prime Minister is saying 'absolutely' in my ear. Mr. Speaker, we will end the feudal leasehold system, which has left millions of homeowners subject to unfair costs and unreasonable practices. Our reforms include clear standards for repairs and maintenance, and this will give homeowners a greater say in how their homes are managed. And I know the housing minister will have heard what he said.

Well, I've said the situation in Birmingham Council is completely unacceptable. But he might want to tell his constituents that we've delivered two million extra appointments for the NHS, so waiting lists are coming down for his constituents. We've delivered the national living wage, a 1,400 pound increase, including for his constituents. We've got record investment into this country, growing the economy, including for his constituents.

Well, I'm grateful for her question. We will unlock growth across the country in partnership with local leaders and giving powers to those with skin in the game. And we'll fix the North's broken transport system, another thing they left in a complete mess, with nearly 1.7 billion pounds for local buses, for roads, and for trams, and an additional 415 million to upgrade the Trans-Pennine route and fixing millions of potholes. And obviously I'll consider her kind invitation.

As in our previous exchange, obviously the unfunded promises, fantasy promises of the party opposite meant his hospital would never have been delivered. They shouldn't moan, they should apologize to his constituents. We had to take tough decisions to make the program deliverable, which is what we've done. We will continue to support the trust to maintain facilities in advance of the new hospital investment, and the minister for secondary care will be visiting the hospital, and that will be an opportunity I hope for the necessary discussions.

Well, I'm very pleased to say, Mr. Speaker, the first 750 breakfast clubs will open this month. And I'm pleased there's an early adopter in his constituency as well as in the constituency of the Leader of the Opposition. I'm sure she will welcome that, one of these weeks. Mr. Speaker, that will put 450 pounds a year back in the pocket of working people. And Mr. Speaker, today we've awarded 37 million pounds to 300 primary schools to create up to 4,000 nursery places from September, making it easier for working families to access government-funded childcare.

Well, I'm grateful to him for raising... I do take a personal interest. I went to Scunthorpe to talk to the management and the workers there a short while ago and understand firsthand the challenges and how deeply worrying it will be for those working there and their families and the community as a whole. And that's why there are negotiations. I do call on the company to accept the offer of financial support that has been advanced so we can achieve a sustainable future for the workforce, for the industry, and the local community, because I do believe there's a bright future for steel and needs to be a bright future for steel. And I do take a personal interest in it.

Mr. Speaker, we are focused on delivering real results for patients by scrapping unnecessary targets, bringing back the family doctor, and requiring online bookings to help the 8:00 AM scramble. We're investing an additional 889 million pounds to reinforce the front door of our NHS, and that's the biggest increase for over a decade. And that will mean hundreds more GPs since we came to power. And this week we've announced record investment for community pharmacies to deliver more services for patients and free up GP time.

Can I thank him for raising this tragic case? And I do pay tribute to the families. Often in cases like this, including this case, I find it hard to think how I would actually respond if I was a family member in circumstances like that. I'm not sure I'd have the courage that they have to campaign in the way they campaigned, and I pay tribute to it. We do need to get to the bottom of all of the issues here, wherever they may lie, and that's what we will do.

Well, Mr. Speaker, she's right. Over 60,000 Scots have been stuck waiting for tests or treatment for over a year. That's a 46% rise in one year. I had to check that figure because it's so staggering. 46% rise in one year. And despite this backlog, almost 50,000 fewer operations are being carried out compared with before the pandemic. Mr. Speaker, compare that to England where we've driven down waiting lists with over two million extra appointments and scrapped NHS England to cut bureaucracy. Scotland's NHS is in desperate need of reform, but the SNP have no strategy, no plans, and no ideas.

I'm happy to tell anyone why the 22 billion pound black hole left in the last... they crashed the economy, they ruined our public services. And as we mend that and rebuild the country, they carp from the sidelines. And even now, they can't bring themselves to say they don't want the investment, they can't bring themselves to say they'll reverse the decisions we've made. They actually agree with the decisions we've made because we're clearing up the mess that they left.

Well, I thank her for raising this appalling incident and our thoughts remain with the families of Jim, of John Chapman, and James Kirby. The attacks on aid workers, Mr. Speaker, are never justified. The families do deserve justice. We're pressing the Israeli government to accelerate their investigation, including whether criminal proceedings should be initiated. Can I also say Israel must stop blocking aid into Gaza, hostages must be released, and we must have an urgent resumption of the ceasefire.

I'm grateful to him for raising this appalling case, and I absolutely agree with him that there must be maximum penalties for anyone falling into that category. I've seen many of these cases for myself firsthand when I was prosecutor for five years working with the police on, you know, really terrible cases and know the impact that it has on victims. I thank him for raising it.

Question 1. Minister. Mr. Speaker, the entire House will join me in paying tribute to His Holiness Pope Francis, an extraordinary man. His lifelong work on fairness will leave a lasting legacy, and people of all backgrounds and beliefs were inspired by his humility and his compassion. And I think the outpouring of grief and love that we've seen in the last two days or so shows the respect and admiration that he's held in around the world. Mr. Speaker, I will attend his funeral on Saturday and pay tribute to his courage and to his leadership. May his holiness rest in peace. Mr. Speaker, may I also wish everyone in England a very happy St. George's Day. There is a lot to celebrate: our history, our values, and our culture. Mr. Speaker, this morning I had meetings with ministerial colleagues and others. In addition to duties in this House, I shall have further such meetings later today.

Mr. Speaker, that's very... well, look, may I start by wishing Jenny, his guide dog, a very happy birthday, I think for yesterday. Six years old, and she doesn't look particularly interested in my answer, I have to say. Mr. Speaker, look, I do recognize the importance of tourism to his beautiful constituency. I've been there many times, worked there for a short time, and driving growth and creating jobs. We've announced a new Visitor Economy Advisory Council, which will work with business, deliver a new strategy focused on supporting growth and the tourism industry. Visit Britain has also launched a new international marketing campaign to showcase Britain's incredible heritage, culture, and landscapes, and I know the Minister of Tourism would be happy to keep him updated.

Well, Mr. Speaker, the honorable friend knows my personal commitment to delivering justice for victims of crime who've been completely failed over the last 14 years. We are improving access to compensation through better online systems and equipping staff with the skills they need to better support victims. We are, of course, also consulting on a revised victims' code that will increase the powers of the Victims' Commissioner to ensure more accountability, and I'm happy to ensure that she meets the relevant minister to discuss those issues.

Well, Mr. Speaker, let me be clear, I welcome the Supreme Court ruling on this issue. It brings clarity and it will give confidence to women and of course to service providers. The Equality and Human Rights Commission will now issue updated guidance, and it's important that that happens and that all service providers then act accordingly. This government's approach and my approach has been as follows: to support and implement the Supreme Court ruling and we will, to continue to protect single-sex spaces based on biological sex and we will, but also to ensure that trans people are treated with respect and we will, and to ensure that everybody is given dignity in their everyday lives. I do think this is the time now to lower the temperature, to move forward and to conduct this debate with the care and compassion that it deserves, and I think that should unite the whole House.

Mr. Speaker, I've always approached this on the basis that we should treat everyone with dignity and respect, whatever their different views. And I'll continue to do so. And I'll tell you, Mr. Speaker, for why. Because when we lose sight of that approach and make this a political football, as happened in the past, then we end up with the spectacle of a decent man, and he was a decent man, the previous Prime Minister, diminishing himself at this dispatch box by making trans jokes whilst the mother of a murdered trans teenager watched from the public gallery just up there. That will never be my approach. My approach will be to support the ruling, to protect single-sex spaces and treat everybody with dignity and respect. And I believe there's a consensus in this House and the country for that approach.

Mr. Speaker, the only fiction here is the idea she delivered anything in office. She held the post of Minister for Women and Equalities for two years, and she did precisely nothing. She provided no clarity on the law, did nothing to improve women's lives, which got materially worse under her watch. They talk, for example, about hospitals and mixed-sex wards. Up hill and down dale, what happened in the last decade? The use of mixed-sex wards in our NHS rose by 2,000%. And there's a pattern of behavior here. Women and Equalities Minister failed to do anything for women. The Trade Minister who failed to get a trade deal with the US. The Business Minister who failed to get a deal with British Steel. She's a spectator, not a leader.

Well, I think the WhatsApp group she should be worried about is the one of his Shadow Justice Secretary. And Mr. Speaker, the mask has slipped just one week before the elections because the Shadow Justice Secretary is not here, a man who's doing everything he can to replace her. The man that most of them want as leader of their party has admitted that reform and the Tories are working together. He said, he said, I want this fight to be united. He said, he said, he's determined to bring this coalition, he calls it, together one way or another. Well, I think we know what that means. Every Tory voter is appalled at the thought of paying for the NHS, every Reform voter who hates what the Tories did in the last 14 years. They're not Conservatives, they're a con.

Mr. Speaker, I've always said the debate should be conducted properly on the principles of debate. I've said it many, many times. But I would remind the leader of the opposition that when they were in government, violence against women and girls reached record highs, rape prosecutions fell to record lows, and millions of women were left stuck on NHS waiting lists unable to get the healthcare that they needed. Under this Labour government, NHS waiting lists down by more than 200,000, domestic abuse specialists in 999 control rooms, we've strengthened access to maternity pay, something she calls excessive. And she talks about political footballs, but a coalition between Reform and the Tories being formed behind her back, we know what that means when the Shadow Justice Secretary and the member for Clacton cook up their joint manifesto. NHS charging, a pro-Russia foreign policy, end to workers' rights. Just as her government lost control of the economy, the borders, and health in six short months, she's lost control of her party.

I can only assume that sounded better when she did it in the mirror earlier on. But the truth is, it doesn't really matter what the leader of the opposition says because nobody believes, none of them, that she's going to lead them into the next election anyway. It's going to be the Shadow Justice Secretary. He's away plotting, that's why he's not here today, Mr. Speaker. And the member for Clacton fighting over the bones of the Tory party, and they think Reform are going to give them their votes without changing their policy? Absolutely no way. The member for Clacton's going to do what he always does, eat the Tory party for breakfast. Drew Pakes.

Well, can I thank my honorable friend. The net-zero transition is a huge economic opportunity for this country, despite the naysayers on the opposition benches. And we've had almost 44 billion pounds of investment since July, and that'll deliver jobs across the country including in his constituency, investment presumably they don't want. We're ensuring we've got skilled workers that we need, launching the Skills England and a new growth and skills offer to encourage even more apprenticeships and supporting industry-led plan for hydrogen to deliver the workforce needed for the industry of the future.

Mr. Speaker, the previous program of the party opposite was undeliverable and unaffordable, as I think he knows and accepts. We put the new hospital program on a sustainable footing with a timeline that can be met. We're not prepared to trade on false promises as they did, and obviously we put record investment into the NHS. But I do just gently urge him to one day get a bit more serious about the funding of these measures because every week he comes here to basically push me on two issues: to spend a lot more money, but at the same time in the next breath, opposing the measures in the budget to raise the money that's necessary.

Well, he raises a really important point of real interest and importance to farmers. We will negotiate, as he would expect, in the national interest and uphold the highest animal welfare standards. We are making progress on that, and then there'll be a process if a deal is reached. Catherine Atkinson.

Mr. Speaker, she's a fantastic champion for Derby. She's right, whether it's the workforce I met at Alstom or the workers at Hitachi in County Durham, we will support our rail industry, providing certainty that delivers jobs, investment, and security for them. I met these workforces, I know how worried they were a year ago, she rightly says, when this government was in charge. I'm really proud that Derby will be the home of Great British Railways because we're bringing railways back into public ownership to deliver better services for passengers, cutting delays and cancellations, and boosting growth across the country. Robin Swann.

Oh, well, I thank him for that question, and I did work in Northern Ireland for five years and therefore appreciate firsthand how important these issues are, and it was a very formative period for me in terms of my career and my thinking. The Good Friday Agreement is one of the proudest achievements of the last Labour government. I pay tribute to everybody, everybody who helped bring that around because, as he will know and other members will know, it was such an important, important moment in the history of the conflict, and I absolutely stand four-square behind the principles, some of which I was doing my part to help implement when I was working in Northern Ireland. They will always drive me on the issues that he raises with me. Andy McDonald.

Well, Mr. Speaker, we are reforming a broken system, the system that we inherited, and I think most people accept that it needs reform because it traps people in unemployment and inactivity, and we need to reform it for that reason. The principles will be that we will provide support where support is needed. Where people do want to get into work, we will help them into work. The current system operates against people getting into work who want to make that transition. And that if you can work, you should work. Moving into work is what halves your risk of being in poverty, and that's why we've invested 1 billion pounds into tailored employment support. And of course we're introducing a new premium for those with the most severe lifelong disabilities who will never be able to work. Jessica Morden.

She raised a really important issue in relation to Port Talbot, and I've visited a number of times and heard firsthand from the workforce there. And she may or may not know that even in opposition before the election, I was talking to the owners to try to persuade them to delay their decisions because I knew an election was coming. That's how important I thought it was. I would remind her that at the same time, the then-Prime Minister refused to pick up a call to the First Minister to even discuss the issue. I took a different approach because I realized just how important it was. I would remind her, because she compares it with the decisions we took last week, that the blast furnaces were turned off in January of last year, the coke ovens in March 2024, and therefore that was before the election. That was the very thing I was trying to ensure didn't happen for reasons that she and the workforce will understand, and I was talking to the workforce throughout that. What we've been able to do then since then is to negotiate an improved deal with Tata. We did that within 10 weeks, better terms for the workers, and we're working hard to maximize opportunities from the 1.25 billion pounds investment in electric arc furnace and supporting those with job losses with 80 million pounds of funding to learn new skills, supply chains, and protect communities. But I mean, she talks about protecting working people, but she voted against the biggest settlement, devolution settlement since devolution. That includes more money for public services including the NHS, and they voted against it. Blair McDougall.

My honorable friend is a real champion for Airdrie and Shotts. And over 60,000 Scots have been stuck waiting for tests or treatments for over a year. That's a 46% rise in one year. And yet almost 50,000 fewer operations are being carried out compared with before the pandemic. And compare what the SNP are doing with what we're doing here in England. We're driven down waiting lists within six months, six months' worth of reductions in a row with over 3 million extra appointments. Scotland's NHS urgently needs change, but the SNP has no strategy, no plan, and absolutely no ideas. Zöe Franklin.

Mr. Speaker, I've set out our approach to China a number of times. It's not materially different to the approach of the last government or the last years of the last government, I might just add. And in relation to Scunthorpe, of course, the deal that we had to deal with during the recess was the deal negotiated by the last government. We've taken sensible decisions in the national interest and will continue to do so. Marie Tidball.

Well, I'm deeply sorry to hear about Billy's case, and I'm sure the whole House is. And our focus has to be on making sure GPs spend more time caring for patients, and that includes the investment of an additional 889 million pounds into general practice in England and putting over 1,500 GPs into surgeries since October. We did deliver a record settlement for Scotland's public service to help fix our NHS and ensure people like Billy get the care that they deserve. John Glen.

Well, look, he's right that we need to go further and faster in terms of kickstarting growth, attracting the investment that we need to create jobs, and our regulators must regulate for growth and not just for risk. And we do want that continuity of leadership that he mentioned, and we are convening and getting people together to drive that growth, and we'll take away the ideas that he puts on the table. Alison Hume.

Well, thank her for her question. I know this means a lot to her. We're clear on the principles for reform: protecting those with the most severe disabilities who will never be able to work, as she references, and making sure people with the most severe disabilities and health conditions will never face the prospect of being constantly reassessed again. We are making sure that extra financial support is based on the impact of health condition or disability, not the capacity to work, and I can reassure her we're carefully considering options for transitional protection. Dave Doogan.

Does he understand the electorate in Scotland answered that question in July of last year? I remember there used to be quite a few of them sitting around here, now it's a distant cry from up there. Final questions.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday evening, Royal Air Force Typhoons successfully conducted strikes against Houthi military targets in Yemen in a joint operation with our US allies. This action was in line with long-standing policy of the UK government to defend freedom of navigation in the Red Sea after Houthi attacks fueled regional instability and risked economic security for families in the UK. Mr. Speaker, I'm pleased to say that all UK aircraft and personnel returned safely, and I pay tribute to the professionalism and bravery of all our servicemen and servicewomen. The Defense Secretary, Mr. Speaker, is making a statement immediately after PMQs. Mr. Speaker, can I congratulate Prime Minister Mark Carney on his election in Canada? Our two countries are the closest of Commonwealth allies, partners, and friends, and we will work together to deepen our economic relationship to benefit working people here in the UK. Mr. Speaker, may I also congratulate everyone across the House, including members of this House and the press gallery, who ran marathons in London and Manchester? In particular, the honorable member for Gordon and Buchan for the fastest run of any female MP. And of course, the Shadow Justice Secretary, who I'm reliably informed is still running. Mr. Speaker, this morning, I had meetings with ministerial colleagues and others. In addition to my duties in this House, I shall have further such meetings later today.

Well, Mr. Speaker, can we extend our congratulations to his daughters for running the marathon? In relation to trade deals, the government retains the right obviously to strike trade deals delivering growth, jobs, and opportunities for working people. We clearly set that out in our manifesto. That's exactly what we're doing. Parliament, as he knows, does have a well-established role in scrutinizing and ratifying these deals, and as he knows, that was strengthened under the last Labour government as he references.
Well, it's not for me to answer, nor responsibility for any pact. Right, let's move to the Leader of the Opposition, Kim Leadbeater.

Mr. Speaker, this is obviously a serious issue. I oversaw the first grooming gang prosecution, which was in Rochdale more than a decade ago. There is a contrast here because the Leader of the Opposition, when she was Minister for Children, Women and Equalities, never raised this issue in the House in three years. Mr. Speaker, the Shadow Home Secretary held 352 external meetings during 20 months. How many were on this issue? Not one. And they failed, of course, to implement a single recommendation from the independent inquiry into child sexual abuse. Mr. Speaker, my position is absolutely clear: where there's evidence, the police should investigate and there should be appropriate prosecutions. That's route number one. Route number two, we should implement existing recommendations which did expose what went wrong. They weren't, those recommendations were not implemented by the last government; they're being implemented by this government. We are providing for local inquiries. We're investing more and delivering truth and justice for victims than the party opposite did in 14 long years.

Mr. Speaker, we are providing for local inquiries. This is a serious... Well, they've got so much to say now. Why did they not, Mr. Speaker, why did they not implement a single recommendation in the 14 years they had in office? We're taking forward the recommendations already in place about the change that needs to be taken. They sat on a shelf under the last government. We are acting on them. We are providing for local inquiries, and we're investing more in delivering truth than they ever did.

Mr. Speaker, I spent five years prosecuting these cases. I was the prosecutor that brought the first case. And when that file was brought to my attention, Mr. Speaker, I noticed that one of the defendants had not been prosecuted previously. Far from covering up, I asked for that file so that I could have a look at it. On the back of that, I then changed the entire approach to prosecutions, which was then lauded by the government we were doing the right thing and brought those prosecutions. So my record, my record was going after where I thought something had gone wrong and putting it right. She stayed silent throughout their years in government, and so did the entire front bench.

Mr. Speaker, we've had a national inquiry. We've had recommendations. There are hundreds of recommendations that have been made in relation to this issue. It is a serious issue. I strongly believe that we should implement the recommendations that have already been made, and that is what we are doing. I strongly believe we should listen to victims, and we've been listening to victims on this side for decades and working with victims for decades in relation to what they want, which is local inquiries, and we've set those local inquiries up.

The right thing is to implement the recommendations that we've got, which is what they palpably failed to do in government. The right thing to do is to have the local inquiries that we need, which is what the victims want. The right thing to do is to invest in our criminal justice system so we can bring people to justice. They've absolutely collapsed the criminal justice system. Prosecutions for rape under their watch, they went up or down? They went down to record lows. Investment in prosecuting these cases went down. Their record was abysmal. They should hang their heads in shame.

She says they'd have a national inquiry. 14 years, 14 years and they didn't do it. It's so hollow. And yes, tomorrow is the first opportunity the country has to pass their verdict on the Leader of the Opposition and the party opposite after a general election. Have they changed? Have they learned? It's passing verdict on the Leader of the Opposition. We'll see you next week.

Well, she's absolutely right to raise the disgraceful record of the previous government, which saw an extra 900,000 children in poverty. I'm proud of Labour's record in reducing child poverty, which is what we do in government, and the task force is exploring every lever to reduce child poverty.

Mr. Speaker, we are in negotiations with the US in relation to a deal. We will act obviously in the national interest and make sure that if there is a deal, it's the right deal for our country. If it is secured, it'll go through the known procedures for this House.

Well, um, I thank him for raising that terrible case, and I think the thoughts of the whole House will be with Christopher's family and friends affected by this. And we'll certainly look into what else we can do, and if there's further details that can be given to me of the particular case, I'll make sure that we follow it up.

Can I add my congratulations to Truro? Clean energy investments are powering our plan for change, Mr. Speaker, and that's just the beginning. We'll go further. 200 schools and hundreds of NHS sites across the country will benefit from GB Energy's first solar projects, including Falmouth Community Hospital in my honorable friend's constituency. Hospitals will save, Mr. Speaker, 45,000 pounds a year off their energy bills, with that money going back to the front-line services. That's the better future we're building: good for patients, good for jobs, growth, and our energy security.

Mr. Speaker, we are passing a Borders Bill with extensive powers to smash the gangs. These are terrorist-like powers that give powers to the police to intercept where they think the suspects are committing people smuggling, which is a vile trade, and we must take back control of our borders after the last government lost control. But what did he and his party do? Did they support those extra measures to actually smash the gangs? No, they went in the lobby with this lot in their new coalition to vote against them. And let's be clear what a vote for his party means: it means a vote to charge for the NHS, it means a pro-Putin foreign policy, and a vote against workers' rights. And now we hear, Mr. Speaker, he's recruited Liz Truss as his new top advisor, and we remember as he was cheering on the mini-budget.

I see the member for Clacton complaining, but what did he say? Said we're going to have to move to an insurance-based system of healthcare. His words: 'if you can afford it, you pay'. Not under our watch, Mr. Speaker. While he's busy taking Liz Truss's advice and falling over Putin, we're driving down waiting lists, three million extra appointments delivered, and waiting lists slashed in the most deprived areas. That's six times the waiting list has come down, including during the winter periods. We're rebuilding our NHS, rebuilding our country of the future, and delivering for working people.

I thank her for raising this, and the party opposite should apologize to her constituents for allowing record sewage into our waterways. Our Water Act will clean up our rivers, lakes, and seas under new powers which came into effect last week, in fact. Water bosses can now face years in jail for concealing sewage spills. We've banned the payment of bonuses and introduced new powers. And of course, we're delivering a major review through our Water Commission. And I'll reassure the member we won't hesitate to take further steps.

The party opposite decimated neighborhood policing, and crimes like shoplifting and anti-social behavior ran riot. I can tell him what we're doing through the plan for change: extra police officers, extra PCSOs, and more special constables. On top of that, Mr. Speaker, a named officer for every community and more teams out in our town centers on Friday and Saturday nights. That's what you get with a Labour mayor working with a Labour government to deliver change for Cambridgeshire and Peterborough.

Can I thank him for raising this important issue with us? We will always stand up for those who served our country and I pay tribute to Pauline for her service, and I will make sure that she gets the appropriate meeting that she wants and needs to discuss her specific case.

Well, look, let me pay tribute to all the staff in her constituency working in the breakfast clubs, which of course, Mr. Speaker, deliver free breakfast clubs, 30 minutes of free childcare, saving working parents 450 pounds a year, and we've opened the first 750 across the country. There'll be many more to come, Mr. Speaker. We are of course also saving parents 50 pounds a year by making school uniforms cheaper, something the Leader of the Opposition ordered all her troops to vote against.

Well, he raises a really important question of anti-social behavior. They're laughing about it. That really sums up what they did in the last 14 years. He knows there are already strict rules in place to prevent anti-social behavior, including fines of up to a thousand pounds. But we are focused on tackling anti-social behavior; it's not low-level, it does affect people and their communities and their sense of safety and what they can do with their own lives. And that's why an additional 1.2 billion has been set aside for policing, 13,000 new neighborhood police officers, new respect orders, and a named officer in every community. We take this seriously, they laugh about it.

She's absolutely right to raise this important issue. Communities across the country are facing the consequences of the utter failure of the party opposite to build enough homes. Our Renters' Rights Bill improves the system for 11 million private renters, blocking demands for multiple months of rent in advance and finally abolishing no-fault evictions, something they said they'd do over and over again and as usual never got round to doing. Mr. Speaker, that's backed up by major planning reforms, our new homes accelerator, and 600 million pounds to deliver 300,000 homes in London, part of our 1.5 million homes we'll build across the country that are desperately needed.

Can I wish him the very best of luck? It will be a fantastic event and it's just one of the many important celebrations that we are that are taking place to commemorate VE Day. I would encourage the whole House to buy those remaining tickets to go along and attend the concert, which I think is in Westminster Hall, as well as the many street parties and other events there will be across the country, and I look forward to paying my own tributes on VE Day. But I wish him luck.

Well, I'm happy to make sure that my honorable friend meets the Health Secretary. Mr. Speaker, we have got waiting lists down for six months now in a row, delivering three million extra appointments. The further, faster 20 program is doubling the rate at which waiting lists are falling, including in her trust. And of course, earlier this week, we froze prescription charges at under 10 pounds. There's a lot that's been done, a lot more to do, but our plan for change is working, getting the NHS back on its feet.

She's right to highlight the misuse of NDAs, and I don't think anybody would countenance the misuse of NDAs, particularly in a case as serious as the one that she cited, which is why we're looking whatever we can do to make sure they're not misused.

Thank you for raising this issue. Under the last government, we saw a million incidents of fly-tipping. Under Conservative councils, we've seen enforcement down and fly-tipping up. Look at Tory-led Northumberland, where instances of fly-tipping are up 76%. We're introducing, Mr. Speaker, tough powers to seize and crush the vehicles of commercial fly-tippers who now face up to five years in prison for operating illegally. That's a Labour government clearing up the mess left by the party opposite.

Always a pleasure. But look, I mean, I can congratulate him on his campaign; it is really important. And many people would be delighted, I think, to join that campaign. Dame Vera is sewn into our nation's soul, providing the soundtrack for our greatest generation. And so it's particularly timely, so I'll support the campaign that he has done so much to promote.

Well, he's absolutely right. Conservative Derbyshire County Council is home to more potholes than anywhere else in the country, and drivers are paying the price. Mr. Speaker, our plan for change is committed enough funding to fix seven million extra potholes this year. And for the first time, councils like Derbyshire must publish how many potholes they've actually repaired in order to get the cash. The party opposite left Britain's roads crumbling; we are fixing them.

Well, many years on the opposite benches I learned when asking questions at PMQs not just to read the headline on a Wednesday morning but to look at some of the detail. What Tony Blair said is we should have more carbon capture. We've invested in carbon capture; that's many jobs across different parts of the country. He said that AI should be used. We agree with that; we've invested huge amounts in AI and the jobs of the future. He also said we need domestic targets so that businesses have their certainty. If you look at the detail of what Tony Blair said, he's absolutely aligned with what we're doing here. These are the jobs and the security of the future. I would also say that we shouldn't weaponize the difficult position that people in Spain and other countries find themselves in at a very difficult time.

Can I pay tribute to my honorable and gallant friend for his service to his country? He understands our national security and economic security go hand in hand. Mr. Speaker, it's vital that defense investment creates more jobs, apprenticeships, and opportunities in the Black Country and across the United Kingdom. That's why we've launched a new hub to give up to 12,000 small firms better access to defense contracts, and of course we're raising defense spending, the highest sustained increase since the Cold War, something the party opposite failed to do in 14 years in office. Right, well let the front bench change over.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Rising tensions between India and Pakistan will be of serious concern for many across Britain. We are engaging urgently with both countries, as well as other international partners, encouraging dialogue, de-escalation, and the protection of civilians. Mr. Speaker, Britain will fall silent tomorrow to mark the anniversary of VE Day. It is a day to remember our greatest generation, whose courage and selflessness won a victory over tyranny and evil. Past and present, the service of our armed forces defends our freedom, protects the values that we stand for, and makes this country so proud. Mr. Speaker, the landmark deal we've secured with India is a huge win for working people in this country. After years of negotiation, this government has delivered in months, slashing tariffs, boosting wages, unleashing opportunities for UK business. It's the biggest trade deal the UK has delivered since we left the EU. Mr. Speaker, this morning I had meetings with ministerial colleagues and others. In addition to my duties in this house, I shall have further such meetings later today.

Mr. Speaker, can I send my best wishes and I'm sure the house to Richard and to every family living with cancer for their courage and fortitude. Can I also pay tribute the honorable friend, my honorable friend for Mitcham and Morden for her work to raise awareness of the devastating impact of brain cancer. I'm really proud that our plan for change has already delivered faster diagnosis for more than 80,000 cancer patients. We're rolling out Cancer 360, Mr. Speaker, that's groundbreaking new technology that will slash treatment delays across the NHS, investing in more scanners, surgical hubs, and radiotherapy machines. It's important work that is only happening because of our decision to make a record investment in the NHS, opposed by every other party.

Mr. Speaker, the number one job of this government was to put our finances back in order after the last government lost control. That is and to deal with the 22 billion black hole that they left.
