Because of our action, we've stabilized the economy, we've invested record amounts in the NHS, we're a payment out for the 3 million lowest paid, and of course we're committed to the triple lock which improved pensions by 470 pounds last year. And Mr. Speaker, because of the work that we've done, we're a country that countries like India want to do deals with because of the messages and the work that we've done.

Mr. Speaker, let's spell this out. All the parties opposite would take this country back to where it was a few years ago. Broken public finances, interest rates through the roof, NHS waiting lists at all-time highs. Because no other party in this house is prepared to say how they would put the finances straight. No other party is saying how they would invest in our NHS and public services. No other party is focused on the long-term prosperity of Britain. No one on this side, Mr. Speaker, is denying how big the challenges that we face, but no one on that side of the house is even prepared to take those challenges on.

Mr. Speaker, the way to bring energy bills down for good is to deliver cheap, clean, homegrown energy. And in the meantime, in the meantime, we've extended the warm homes discount to 6 million households, one in five families. That's 150 pounds off the bills next winter. But what won't bring energy bills down is the leader of the opposition's policy, leaving us hooked on fossil fuels at the mercy of dictators like Putin. I'll tell you what else won't bring bills down, it's them blocking every infrastructure that's needed in their own backyard. They balance the books, they crash the economy on the backs of millions of working people in this country. That's why they delivered the verdict they did at the last general election.

Energy bills on fossil fuel have fluctuated massively in the last three years because we're exposed to the international market. The only way, the only way to get bills down is to go to renewable energy. It's something she used to believe in, Mr. Speaker. Her, and Mr. Speaker, I've got the Shadow Chancellor here, his previous words. 'Net zero, the shift must happen now as a matter of urgency.' His words. 'It's no longer environmental issue. Energy independence should be reviewed as part of our national security.' He must have our lines, I think Mr. Speaker. But what about the leader of the opposition herself? This is what she said: 'We believe that green trade and investment will be the future-proofing force that will help us create better tomorrow.' And then she went on to say this Mr. Speaker: 'It's long-term investment in nuclear and renewables that will reduce our dependencies on fossil fuels and keep down consumer costs.' Now she's got a reputation apparently for straight talking, she was right then, wasn't she?

Mr. Speaker, as I've said many times, oil and gas will be part of the mix for many decades to come. But net zero, Mr. Speaker, is an opportunity to be seized. We've had over 43 billion pounds invested since July of last year in clean energy. That's good for the economy, good for business, good for jobs, apprentices, and growth. Mr. Speaker, the global race is on for the jobs of the future, and I believe Britain can win that race. The leader of the opposition, I don't think is yet a climate denier, but she's a climate defeatist. She doesn't believe in Britain's ability to win the race for our economy, businesses and jobs. And they've never backed Britain, there's nothing patriotic about that.

Mr. Speaker, of course nobody wants to see job losses. But she should, she should address her comments to the tens of thousands of men and women in this country working on renewables for the future of our country and tell them that she doesn't want them. That is anti-growth, anti-jobs and anti-working people. But every week, Mr. Speaker, she comes along to talk the country down, to carp from the side. She can't even bring herself to celebrate the deal we've done with India. They took eight years fiddling around and got absolutely nothing. We've delivered the best deal since we left the EU, the most ambitious deal for India, which will be measured in billions of pounds into our economy and thousands of jobs in the country. She should be welcoming that.

Mr. Speaker, he makes a very good point. We are backing British car companies like JLR and our India trade deal will see tariffs slashed for car sales and that is good for British jobs. And the criticism on the double taxation is incoherent nonsense. It's a benefit to working people, it's in the agreements that we've already got with 50 other countries. And if the member for Clacton or the leader of the opposition is seriously suggesting that they're going to tear up agreements with 50 other countries and create a massive hole in our economy, they should get up and they should say so.

Mr. Speaker, as he knows, we've taken this in two stages, we are already taking measures to increase the support for social care quite right too and doing the long work to reform and make sure we put a system in place. But can I just say to him once again, he comes here every week saying we should spend more money and he comes here at the same time saying he doesn't want to pay for any of the measures to raise that money. That is nonsense.

Mr. Speaker, he really should listen to the sectors that he thinks he's championing. They do not want us to abandon the work we're doing to try and get an agreement with America. They want that agreement to reduce tariffs. That's the sensible pragmatic way to protect our national interest. It is not sensible or pragmatic to choose between the US and the EU, to abandon the work we're doing on trade with the US and leave the tariffs exactly where they are. That's the most damaging thing that could possibly be done.

Well Mr. Speaker, it's good to see a local Labour MP fighting for jobs in his constituent and achieving excellent results. Mr. Speaker, we will make our final investment decision at the spending review. Something the party opposite failed to deliver in 14 years. We're unashamedly pro-nuclear, pro-growth and pro-jobs. That's why we're making it easier to build small modular reactors and scrapping absurd rules that left vital projects tangled up in needless paperwork. We're doing the work that they failed to do in 14 years.

Mr. Speaker, nobody wants to see job losses. But I'd remind the right honorable member that before we came into office 10 months ago, the SNP government in Holyrood alongside the Conservative government did absolutely nothing for projects like Grangemouth. Absolutely nothing. At Grangemouth we have committed 200 million pounds to secure the future for the site, delivered 100 million pound deal and we're helping with the training guarantees that are needed. But just like his first minister, the honorable well he'll raise anything to distract from their disastrous record. Almost one in six Scots stuck on an NHS waiting list, standards and violence in Scottish schools, over a billion pounds cut from local government. We gave them the biggest settlement since devolution. They've been in power for nearly two decades, they've got absolutely nowhere to hide for their appalling record.

She's absolutely right Mr. Speaker. Royal Barrow is a model for how defense can be a catalyst for the skilled well-paid jobs right across the United Kingdom. And I was proud and humbled to thank the crew of the Vanguard submarine returning home after months away including four of those on board who were returning to their newborn children. That's the change that will come from spending 2.5% of GDP on defense for the first time since the last Labour government. Extra investment in Barrow's been made possible by my honorable friend and this government because the party opposite made promises but as usual they never ever set the money aside.

Well can I thank her for raising this really important issue? And I'm sure members across the house would support a memorial to the service and sacrifice of those veterans. The bravery and service of individuals like Captain Tilley and others in the photographic reconnaissance units and photographic interpreters saved the lives of many servicemen and servicewomen and of course civilians at the cost as she rightly points out of many casualties in fact to those units. So as we mark the 80th anniversary of VE Day we will remember them who helped secure our greatest victory.

Well she's absolutely right. Families are desperate for security of their own home and we are delivering the biggest boost to affordable and social housing in a generation backed by an additional 2 billion pounds of investment. That and our reforms will supply our ambitions to build 88,000 new homes across London including in her constituency. Mr. Speaker at the same time we're tackling the root causes of homelessness and of course scrapping section 21 evictions.

Well she's right to raise the appalling record of the last government which saw 900,000 more children in poverty. Mr. Speaker we're already delivering 750 free breakfast clubs, boosting the minimum wage for over 3 million that's the lowest paid workers in our country and the child poverty task force is looking at every lever that can be pulled. I'm very proud of the last Labour government's record on tackling poverty and we'll continue to do that in this government.

Well I thank her for raising this issue. The contrast as she points out is stark. In England and Wales waiting lists are falling with over 3 million extra appointments already delivered. In Scotland the SNP have introduced, they've just introduced Mr. Speaker their fifth NHS recovery plan in just four years. They've had the biggest budget settlement since devolution, nearly two decades in power, they've still no idea how to fix the NHS and they've run out of excuses.

Well I thank her for raising the record of the postwar Labour government, a great reforming government. Mr. Speaker the principles remain the same which is those that need support and protection should have that support and protection. Those that can be supported and helped into work should be helped and supported into work, something that isn't happening under the system as it is. And those who can work should work.

Well Mr. Speaker he's right to highlight the importance of stronger and more reliable rail connections improving journeys and driving economic growth. The party opposite utterly failed to grip delivery on HS2. Costs went through the roof, timelines were shredded, false promises and a total failure. Mr. Speaker we're reviewing the position that we inherited and we're committed to improving rail connectivity across the north and we've already announced 415 million pounds extra for the key Transpennine route upgrade which will slash journey times deliver growth and a more reliable modern service for passengers.

Well Mr. Speaker most of what he says is simply not right. But can I address I do want to address the position in Gaza and the West Bank because it is increasingly intolerable. And I am deeply concerned particularly with the lack of aid that is getting in and the impact it's having on tens of thousands hundreds of thousands of individuals. That concern is something I recently reaffirmed to the Prime Minister of the Palestinian Authority where I asserted again that a two-state solution is the only viable approach for peace. And our focus is on delivering peace for Palestinians and Israelis, returning to the ceasefire, getting the hostages out and humanitarian aid in that is desperately needed in greater number and more quickly.

Well Mr. Speaker I'm deeply sorry to hear about Martin's case and absolutely agree with her comments about every family deserving a safe and a secure home. And in England that's why we're investing an additional 2 billion pounds to help deliver the biggest increase in social and affordable house building in a generation. But in Scotland it is frankly disgraceful that over 10,000 children have no fixed home to call their own after nearly 20 years of an SNP government. Mr. Speaker that's the highest level ever and shows why Scotland desperately needs a new direction.

Mr. Speaker nobody likes pubs better than me and we support them. But Mr. Speaker it's the same old nonsense. They say they don't want the National Insurance rise but they don't have the courage to say they'd reverse it because they know if they said that they wouldn't be able to say where the money's coming from. That's how we got into the problem in the first place.

Well Mr. Speaker can I join her and commend all the staff at Smile for their vital work. Far too many young people are left without the support that they need and that's why we're recruiting an additional 8,500 mental health workers providing access to specialist mental health professionals in every school and funding talking therapies across the country to bring down waiting times and get people the care they need.

Mr. Speaker as she knows we're committed to resetting the relationship with the EU. We think there's a better deal that can be had. I'm not going to provide a running commentary. What I can say is this, it will be we will act only as we always do in the national interest. We've secured a very good deal with India, we're talking to the US, and we're going for a reset with the EU to boost our economy.

Well Mr. Speaker he raises a really important point. We enjoy free press and independent journalism in this country. Across the world journalists risk their lives and lose their lives doing what they do best independently pursuing the truth. And I've been on many a occasion to award ceremonies usually on a yearly basis where the names of those journalists who have either lost their lives or their freedom is read out and it's always a humbling reminder of the really important work that they do.

Mr. Speaker I'm really proud that on our planning and infrastructure we're taking the action that hasn't been taken for years to drive our economy and I'd remind him it was the thing that was signaled by the OBR as the single biggest driver of growth over the coming year.

Mr. Speaker, over the past week we've secured a historic trade deal with India and a landmark agreement with the United States, protecting and creating British jobs, slashing tariffs and driving economic growth. We've also published a white paper setting out how this government will end the open borders experiment of the party opposite, bringing net migration down, backing British workers and delivering fair control of our borders. Mr. Speaker, I know the whole house will also want to mark the 40th anniversary of the Bradford City fire. We remember the victims of that devastating tragedy and celebrate the strength of the community. Mr. Speaker, this morning I had meetings with ministerial colleagues and others. In addition to my duties in this house, I shall have further such meetings later today.

Mr. Speaker, I love the fact that when anyone says 14 years of a Conservative government, they all go "oh no". That's how the country feels. Mr. Speaker, once again, a hardworking Labour MP clearing up the mess that was left behind. Her residents deserve far better. We expect rapid improvements, we're closely monitoring air quality and won't hesitate to take further action. She's right, we must tackle rogue operators who blight our communities. That's why we've boosted Environment Agency funding by 188 million pounds, alongside tough new rules on incinerators and commercial fly-tippers.

Mr. Speaker, can I pay tribute to Roy Stone as well, and the service that was given in various capacities. Can I thank her for her words about the attacks on me and my family, and the kind messages from many others in the last few days. She did actually message me pretty well straight away, and I really do appreciate that. And she's absolutely right that this is an attack on all of us, on democracy and the values that we stand for. Mr. Speaker, she comes here every week to talk the country down. We've got 200,000 new jobs, record investment, four interest rates cuts. Contrast that with the disastrous Liz Truss mini-budget, inflation through the roof, and a 22 billion pound black hole.

Mr. Speaker, nobody wants to see job losses, but she must be the only person left in the country who thinks the economy was booming under the last government. We've created new jobs, record investment, trade deals that they tried... the India deal I think they tried for eight years and failed, we did that deal. They talked about a US deal, we did that deal. We've built a stronger relationship with the EU. The former Trade Minister must be the only former Trade Minister who's against all trade deals which boost our economy. She says she's against the India deal even though it's got the same provision she put on the table. She's against the US deal even though it saves thousands of jobs in car manufacturing. And Mr. Speaker, most absurdly, she says she's going to rip up the EU deal when she hasn't even seen what's on the page. This is reduced to a brain rot. A once great political party is sliding into brain-dead oblivion.

Mr. Speaker, I think she just said "a tiny tariff deal". Can I suggest that she gets the train to Solihull, two hours, goes to speak to the workforce at JLR, their families and their communities, to tell them she would rip up the deal that protects their jobs? And when she's done that, she might travel across to Scunthorpe and tell the steelworkers there she's going to rip up the deal that saves their jobs. And then if she's got time, go up to Scotland and talk to the whisky distilleries, tell them she'd rip up the deal that's creating 1,200 jobs for them, boosting their exports, and then come back here next week and tell us what reaction she got.

Mr. Speaker, we have provided 100 million pounds boosting for the sector and children and young persons' hospitals receive 26 million pounds funding this year. But Mr. Speaker, she turns up every week to carp from the sidelines. But what she doesn't do, she moans, she moans about what we had to do in the budget to stabilize the economy, but she hasn't got the courage to stand there and say she would reverse the NICs decisions that we take. And I know why, it's because she doesn't want to say she's against the 26 billion pound investment in our NHS. She doesn't want to say she's against the 1.2 billion pound more for our police. She doesn't want to say she's against the 3.2 billion pound more for our schools. All the time she doesn't have the courage of her convictions. It shows that her criticism is totally perfected.

Mr. Speaker, it's the same old Tories. Every time better rights for workers are on the table, they vote against them. Respect and dignity and protection at work are good for workers, good for the economy and good for growth.

Mr. Speaker, she says we should listen to business. They are in favor of our trade deal. The India deal, fantastic deal, tariffs on cars cut to 10%, whisky and gin tariffs halved, 4.8 billion pound into our economy. What does she say she'd do with the India deal? She wants to rip it up. The US deal that saves thousands upon thousands of jobs, what does she want to do? She wants to rip it up. The EU deal, good for our economy, she's not going even wait to see what it says, she absurdly says she's going to rip it up. It is so unserious. She even was reduced last week to calling the Indian government, accusing them of fake news. No wonder she did so badly as a Trade Secretary. Mr. Speaker, the project for them is over, they're sliding into oblivion, they're a dead party walking.

Well, can I pay tribute to her for her work with JLR, standing up for the jobs in her constituency. The deal that we've agreed saves thousands of jobs in our car industry, securing the livelihoods of countless families. And Mr. Speaker, I've been up to JLR on a number of occasions, including last week. I know firsthand what it means for their workforce, for their families and for their communities. And the leader of the opposition says she would go and tell them she's going to rip it up, she says she's going to go against it. The Reform leader said JLR deserves to go bust. Shame on him. Labour is making deals in the national interest.

Can I first thank him for his comments about myself and my family, I do really appreciate it. It is important that we have fair pay for care workers and that's why we've put in place our fair pay agreement. This is the first of its kind, it will be applied first to care workers to ensure that they get fair pay but also a better framework for progression. As he will know, most people leaving care work are leaving care work to go to the NHS because of the pay and the ability to progress. Our fair pay agreements will deal with that and to make sure that in the future those jobs are more secure. And I would just add, Mr. Speaker, declaration of interest, my sister is a care worker and I know firsthand how important the work is and how difficult sometimes the situation is facing them.

Well, I thank him for raising this because the situation in Gaza is simply intolerable and getting worse. And we are working with other leaders urgently to bring about rapid and unimpeded flow of humanitarian aid into Gaza, which is desperately needed, obviously alongside the release of hostages and to get back to a ceasefire. And that work is going on through my team 24/7. I do believe that that is the initial action that needs to be taken, but I still fundamentally believe that however remote it may seem at the moment, the pathway to a two-state solution is the only way for settled and lasting peace in the Middle East, and we will continue with our allies to pursue that path.

Mr. Speaker, everyone enjoying our beautiful beaches, lakes and rivers is entitled to know that the water is clean and safe. That's why we're modernizing outdated bathing water regulations, including more regular monitoring of sites to reflect local demand. And after years of failure by the party opposite, we're acting through our plan for change, through new powers to tackle pollution, including banning bonuses, jail terms for law-breaking bosses and real-time monitors of every sewage outlet.

Yes, the belief that she talks rubbish. Mr. Speaker, I want to lead a country where we pull together and walk into the future as neighbors and as communities, not as strangers. And the loss of control of migration by the last government put all of that at risk. And that's why we're fixing the system based on principles of control, selection and fairness.

Well, I thank my honorable friend. He's been a dedicated campaigner on this for a very long time. As he knows, 14 years of mismanagement by the party opposite left councils on their knees with a total failure to improve and update how councils are funded. Through 69 billion pounds of funding this year and the upcoming multi-year settlement, the first in over a decade, we'll give councils far greater certainty and stability. Our detailed funding review will create a fairer system to make sure his constituents see strong, affordable local services.

Further evidence, Mr. Speaker, of the decline of the Tory party when they say that going to Ukraine at the weekend to try and secure peace for Ukraine and for Europe and the security and defense of Europe is somehow the wrong priority. That conflict has already massively impacted people in this country through the cost of living crisis and energy. Ukraine, Europe and we deserve peace and to live in peace. Mr. Speaker, on the bin strikes, dealing with the bin strikes is the priority. We continue to call on Unite to suspend the strike immediately and bring the disruption to an end. We are supporting the council to ramp up the cleaning operation and now collecting over 1,100 tons of waste every day and continue to offer our support so the backlog doesn't reappear.

I thank my honorable friend, she's a powerful champion on this issue. Our principle is that every young person with special education needs should receive the right support to succeed. We've immediately announced an additional 1 billion pounds for high needs funding, including almost 20 million for schools in Lancashire. We will support special schools and deliver truly inclusive places and expertise in mainstream schools to help every child thrive.

Mr. Speaker, the situation is serious. The last government lost control of the borders. We are taking powers, the Borders Bill is precisely to his point, the Borders Bill is the first bill to give terrorism-like powers to law enforcement precisely so that we can get in before the crimes are committed, before people get to this country. That's why this is the most far-reaching provision ever for law enforcement to defend and secure our borders. And that's why it is extraordinary that he of all people voted against it. Sooner or later he's going to have some explaining to do.

Can I commend my honorable friend, she's led the campaign to highlight the devastating impact of these crimes. Mr. Speaker, for hardworking small businesses, the theft of tools isn't just a violation, it can mean thousands of pounds of potential work lost and with a huge impact to businesses and to families. We're investing over 1.2 billion pounds extra into policing with 13,000 new neighborhood police to focus on crimes that impact on communities the most. And I pay tribute to my honorable friend and I know the Justice Secretary will look at the details carefully.

Can I thank him for his question. As he will know, the Secretary of State is going through a quasi-judicial exercise and therefore I'm limited in what I can say, but let me do the best I can within those constraints because the project is going through its examination where interested parties can put forward their views on the application and should do so. More broadly, as we drive forward renewable projects, the planning process is designed to ensure impacts are carefully considered. Thank you.

The honorable and gallant friend is right that our ironclad support for Ukraine should go hand in hand with firing up our own defense industries. And that means well-paid secure jobs right across the country including in Plymouth and strengthening national security. We reiterated our support for Ukraine in Kyiv last weekend, and I'm proud that British industries are playing their part supporting Ukraine against Russia's illegal invasion. I'll make sure that he meets the relevant minister to discuss his proposal.

Mr. Speaker, only a few years ago dealing with the climate challenge was a shared endeavor across this house. And it's yet further evidence of how far his party has fallen, that they cannot see the significance and importance of tackling one of the major challenges of our time. I think we should rise to that challenge, not be defeatist about it. And it's further evidence as far as I can see that the Tory project is just finished.

Can I thank him for raising this crucial issue. And across the house I know members will have their own personal and tragic experiences of suicide. Mr. Speaker, we've launched a call for evidence on our men's health strategy which will improve men's health in all parts of the country including tackling devastatingly high suicide rates. We're also investing 26 million pounds in new mental health crisis centers, funding talking therapies for 380,000 more people and recruiting 8,500 more mental health workers.

The honorable member's constituents have been badly let down by the previous government's empty promises which were never going to deliver. We've put the new hospitals program on a sustainable financial footing, increasing the NHS capital budget to record levels so we can address the backlog of critical maintenance repairs and upgrades. And I'll make sure that he gets a meeting with the relevant minister to discuss the particular case.

Mr. Speaker, she's a superb champion for energy security, driving down bills and the good secure jobs that renewables offer. And the parties opposite are climate defeatists. Anti-jobs, anti-growth, anti-business and anti-investment. And they should go and peddle their policies to the tens of thousands of people, working people in this country working in renewables every single day. They don't think that Britain has the skills and they would deny us incredible opportunities. We're focused on securing billions in investment, creating tens of thousands of jobs and taking us off the rollercoaster of international fossil fuels.

Can I extend my thoughts to Victor and the awful circumstances that she describes, it must be extremely challenging. We do have to reform the system that we've got, it's not working, I think there's a general agreement about that. But the principles have to be clear, that we protect and secure those that need that protection and security. We help those who can work into work, and those who can work should work. But we have to reform the system that we've got to make it a better system because what we've got doesn't work.

Mr. Speaker, she's absolutely right. Let's be clear what the parties opposite voted against. Stronger statutory sick pay they voted against. The right to guaranteed hours they voted against. Protection from unfair dismissal they voted against. Stronger protection for pregnant mothers they voted against. Insecure work, a package worth 600 pounds to the poorest workers, they voted against. Mr. Speaker, we're backing British workers, they vote against them at every turn.

Mr. Speaker, I'm grateful to him for raising this issue which must be of concern. I'm not across the details of it, I'm afraid at this stage, but I will make sure that he gets a meeting with the relevant minister to get to the bottom of the issue that he's just described.

Can I pay tribute to how he's bringing people together to deliver better care in the community that meets the needs of his constituents? Mr. Speaker, I remind myself they left the NHS on its knees. The last Labour government brought the waiting list down to record lows. They drove them up to record highs. Mr. Speaker, she knows that no Prime Minister or Chancellor ever stands at this dispatch box and writes budgets in the future. And listen to what they did. It isn't what we did. And she knows it. Stephen Flynn.

Well, Mr. Speaker, we've delivered more in the first year of a Labor government than they've delivered in 20 years. Let me give him, let me give him one example. David Taylor.

Joe White.

Mr. Speaker, investors are fleeing the country, fleeing the country. He says he will stick to his manifesto promises. Mr. Speaker, he says he stabilized the economy, has he spoken to any farmers recently? It is time for him to take responsibility for the mess he is making. Well, Mr. Speaker, it's telling that when he raises the question of the broken SEND system, they laugh at the back of the Tory opposition. They laugh. Mr. Speaker, we're working closely with the French on this issue. We'll only provide funding that delivers for our priorities. Mr. Speaker, we are fixing the mess that we inherited. We are working with other countries to ensure that we take the measures necessary to stop people crossing the channel. Well, I'm grateful to him and I've discussed it with him before, he's a brilliant champion for Exeter. Mr. Speaker, every child should have support to realize their potential and the party opposite tore up Sure Start and took it out of our communities, an act in my view of vandalism that abandoned families and deepened inequalities. Mr. Speaker, I'm really not going to take advice from a party that put forward 80 billion pounds of unfunded commitments at the last election. Well, I'm proud that we'll give 15 million workers, that's half of our workforce, stronger rights at work. Both of them vote against reform and better protection of workers at every turn they always have and they always will, they offer nothing for working people.

Well, can I join him in his thanks to the veterans here today with us and to all veterans. In advance of the new legislation the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland continues to engage with veterans and their communities to ensure that legacy mechanisms are fair, that they're lawful and they're proportional and I'll continue to work with him and others in the house because the most important thing is not scoring points but getting it right.

Well, I thank him for that. The party opposite failed to give children the support that they need. The 10-year plan that we've put forward will rewire our NHS and transform mental health services. Eighty-five dedicated mental health A&E departments giving 24/7 support, specialist mental health professionals in every school and college benefiting 1 million young people this year alone and an extra 8,500 mental health staff to tackle long waits and that is only because of the decisions that we took to invest in our NHS, decisions that they opposed.

What, well I thank her for raising this issue and I know it's a concern to her and to many people across the house. Well, it's so good to see strong Labor MPs standing up for Wales and her constituency. Well, Mr. Speaker, another shameful legacy from the party opposite, with one in four adults struggling with NHS care and tooth decay as the most common reason for hospital admissions for children aged five to nine under their watch. We are fixing this, Mr. Speaker, and I can set out what we're doing. We're rolling out 700,000 urgent and emergency appointments, we're reforming the dental contract and recruiting more dentists and newly qualified dentists to practice in the NHS for a minimum period. Mr. Speaker, we are fixing the problem that they inherited. They said they'd take control of borders and they lost it. We're working hard with our allies. Mr. Speaker, she said they're not referring themselves to the ethics advisor. That's part, that's amongst the reasons they got booted out of office last year. Free breakfast clubs, opening new school-based nurseries. That's what we're fighting for, the best start for every child in this country.

Can I join him on his comments about Annette Brooke and also in his description about the horrifying situation in Gaza. That would be catastrophic for dealing with the problem that we're actually dealing with.

I have to say land routes are the only viable and sustainable means of getting aid into Gaza at the scale that is required and Israel must lift the restrictions to allow aid agencies to deliver the life-saving supplies that are so desperately needed.

Mr. Speaker, he overlooks the fact that the last budget there was a record settlement for Scotland, 50 billion pounds a year. And he talks about the support. Well, Mr. Speaker, of course the honorable member for Clacton is not here representing his constituents in the house that he was elected to. Well, I think the whole House is sorry to hear about the awful fires that her constituents have faced, including the destruction of Saint Mungo's and I know just how important that church was, Mr. Speaker, to the local community. The Scottish government have received the largest settlement in the history of devolution, that's 50 billion pounds a year. That should be focused on the issues that matter to her constituents. We now have a returns agreement with France, we wouldn't need a single returns agreement with France if we hadn't ripped up the Dublin agreement.

Well, Mr. Speaker, look, we do stand at an important moment. Well, I thank her for raising this and I was very proud on Monday to make the announcement about childcare. That locks in equality, inequality for life. I'm really pleased that this measure that we've now taken on Monday unlocks that and makes sure every single child age four gets the starting line in reception with a fair chance of going as far as their talents will take them.

Well, Mr. Speaker, I did notice that the leader of the opposition went to Scotland I think this week to announce that if she ever became Prime Minister, which is extremely unlikely, that she would pull down 50 billion pounds of investment in renewables in Scotland. This is good secure jobs of the future, absolutely reckless behavior. They haven't learned anything. Well, and I have met Michael Thomas a number of times. Of course he's got a special place in my heart having scored that winning goal at Anfield when we won the league. I can update the house, Mr. Speaker: retail sales are higher than expected, inflation is lower than expected, growth has been upgraded this year, and Mr. Speaker, the UK stock market is at an all-time high. The budget is on the 26th of November, and we will lay out our plans. But I can tell the house now that we will build a stronger economy, we will cut NHS waiting lists, and deliver a better future for our country.

Mr. Speaker, as she well knows, no Prime Minister or Chancellor will ever set out their plans in advance of the budget. But Mr. Speaker, I can say this, I can say this, Mr. Speaker, because the figures on the productivity review that's being undertaken - this is a judgment on their record in office. Those figures, those figures are now coming through, and they confirm that the Tories did even more damage to the economy than we previously thought. Now we will turn that around. We've already delivered the fastest growth in the G7 in the first half of this year. Five interest rate cuts in a row. Trade deals with the US, EU, and India. They broke the economy, we're fixing it.

Why didn't they do it then in 14 years in office? And Mr. Speaker, as I said, the productivity review figures are now coming in, and they show the true extent of the damage that they did. And as she asks us to take advice from them, we all know austerity damaged the economy on their watch, the botched Brexit deal damaged the economy on their watch, Liz Truss's mini-budget damaged the economy on their watch. So we'll take no lectures or advice from them on the economy. They won't be trusted on the economy for generations to come. And Mr. Speaker, that's why at our budget, I can be clear: there will be no return to austerity - that's what broke the country. No return to the instability of their mad borrowing spree. And we'll end the unfairness and low growth that squeezed living standards for working people. That's the path to national renewal.

Mr. Speaker, she talks about their record. Let's go through it. They crashed the economy. Inflation went up to 11%. Mortgages went through the roof. Welfare spending went up 33 billion pounds on their watch, and they want to give us advice? And they reduced the UK to a laughing stock. Because of our budget, Mr. Speaker, waiting lists have come down, wages are up, mortgage rates are down, and other countries want to do deals with us. Just on Monday of this week, the Turkish government signed an 8 billion pound deal for Typhoons. Earlier this year, the Norway government signed a 10 million pound deal for frigates. That is because of the budget that we passed, fixing the mess that they left.

Mr. Speaker, she's overlooked the fact that we had the highest growth in the G7 the first six months of this year, and that growth's just been upgraded. Three interest rate cuts. But Mr. Speaker, we're not going to take lessons from them. She's now introduced what I understand to be, Mr. - I think she calls it a golden economic rule, this golden rule that she's now putting forward. Very golden. 47 billion pounds, Mr. Speaker, of unspecified spending cuts with no detail whatsoever. Mr. Speaker, let me put that in context. That would be 85,000 fewer nurses, 234,000 fewer teachers, or cutting every police officer in the country twice over. No wonder the Institute for Government said she's on shaky foundations. That's exactly what caused the problem in the first place.

They were kicked out of office because they broke the economy. They won't be trusted for years to come. She can't tell us what her position is on the last budget, and she's got a phantom 47 billion pounds with no foundation as we go forward. That's exactly the mess that they caused. They've not changed one bit. Meanwhile, we're fixing their mess: 5 million extra NHS appointments, five interest rate cuts, growth and wages up. That's a change that a Labour government makes.

Well, I thank him for raising this and I'm deeply concerned, Mr. Speaker, by the strikes and that underlines the fragility of this ceasefire deal. All sides need to uphold President Trump's peace plan. It is the only route to long-term peace for Israelis and Palestinians. We are of course in close touch with the US and regional allies, pushing for de-escalation. Mr. Speaker, the scale of destruction in Gaza is unimaginable. The immediate priority remains getting aid in at the speed and the volume needed. Thank you.

I join his comments on Pernella Scales. And on this question of Russian interference, it is a serious problem in countries across Europe, including in our country, where it's a constant threat. And Mr. Speaker, for NATO allies, the conflict in Ukraine and dealing with Russian aggression is the number one issue. And that is why I have to say the Reform Party would be an absolute disaster for our defense. We are a trusted member of NATO. We wouldn't be a trusted member if we were Putin-friendly. We are leading the coalition of the willing, giving security and comfort to 30 other countries. That would collapse under Reform because they're Putin-friendly, and it would be a real threat to our defense and our security.

Well, he must have overlooked the fact that there was a UK-EU summit earlier this year in which there were 10 strands to the change that we've already agreed in relation to relationship with the EU, including closer trading relationships, including closer work on defense and security, and that is an iterative process that we will continue into next year. But he's absolutely right about the botched deal of the last government, the damage that's done to our economy, and we're just seeing some of the figures come through in relation to that. That's one of the factors behind the way they crashed the economy.

Well, can I start by wishing Hartlepool United the best for this season. He will appreciate the structure of the leagues is a matter for leagues themselves, but I do commend his campaign and everything that he's putting behind it. I also want to pay tribute to the staff, the fans, and the players at Sheffield Wednesday at this difficult time. Mr. Speaker, we've delivered the independent football regulator to stand up for fans and make sure clubs have fit and proper owners. The party opposite used to support that, but now they oppose it.

Well, can I thank him for raising this important issue and I know it is of real concern to him. Can I reassure him that I am in regular contact with the Chief Constable Jon Boucher and the PSNI on this very issue as he would expect. As he is aware, we provided a record settlement for the executive, 19.3 billion pounds per year on average. We also invested 113 million in additional security funding for the PSNI to help address specific security challenges. Now whilst it's for the executive to set the PSNI budget, I want to reassure him that our commitment is to keeping people safe in Northern Ireland.

Well, can I thank him for raising this tragic case, and I'm sure I speak for the whole house in saying we send our sympathies and thoughts to Hudson's parents, Shannon and Tyler. And I'll make sure that they get the meeting that he's asking for. This is exactly why we're working to improve access to face-to-face appointments for those that want one, and to enable that, we've delivered the largest cash uplift for GPs in a decade, put over 2,500 GPs into general practice, and we're upgrading a thousand surgeries to deliver 8 million more appointments.

Well, can I thank him for raising this case and the two examples that he's given. The downgrade at Basildon Hospital is deeply disappointing. The Care Quality Commission has set out immediate actions for the trust leaders to deliver improvements. Our decisions in government have seen 26 billion pound boost for our NHS, helping deliver over 5 million extra appointments. I would gently point out that he was elected representing a Reform Party that would dismantle our NHS and charge people to see their doctor.

I'm proud that we delivered the biggest upgrade to workers' rights in a generation, and the Tories and Reform voted against it at every turn as they always do with any form of workers' rights and protections. And in relation to the deal that we struck on Monday, Mr. Speaker, with Turkey, that is a deal worth 8 billion pounds, 20,000 jobs, 10 years of work in manufacturing with the Typhoons. That is only possible because we're a trusted member of NATO, and Reform would be an absolute nightmare on defense because they would not be a trusted member because they're Putin-friendly.

Well, I thank him for raising this and I know this is personal to him. We are investing 600 million pounds to improve diagnostic capacity and rolling out new radiotherapy machines, including in his local trust, I'm pleased to say. We have seen real improvements: 148,000 more people now have cancer diagnosed or ruled out within 28 days, but I acknowledge there is more to do on this. The National Cancer Plan will set out how we will go further and deliver the best care for every patient.

Well, can I thank him for raising this, and I know how important face-to-face banking is on our high streets. We have committed as he says to rolling out 350 banking hubs across the United Kingdom. Over 180 are already open. I want to reassure him that 350 is not the limit. While decisions over hubs are taken independently, they can be rolled out wherever a community needs one, and I'm happy to make sure the relevant minister follows up with details for him.

Yes, she's bearing down on the challenges the Home Office, most of them inherited from the last government, and we will make the changes necessary and I have every confidence in the Secretary of State to do so.

Can I agree with him. I thought the King and the Pope praying together was an incredible message to the world and very, very powerful. And I agree with him that if we all work together we can actually bring people together notwithstanding the very many difficulties and challenges that that poses around the world and in our own country. It's why so far as we can we should be uniting on national patriotic renewal in this country rather than the toxic division that we see on some of the benches opposite.

Well, my honorable friend's constituency is just one example of why the United Kingdom is a world leader in educating and attracting the brightest minds. Our immigration white paper includes changes to make sure more of the world's best graduates and entrepreneurs start their careers and their businesses here. Mr. Speaker, we're also boosting our R&D sector with more than 86 billion pounds, making sure we continue to attract the best and the brightest.

Mr. Speaker, our small business plan was widely welcomed by small businesses across the country, not least because of their input into it. But she complains about the measures we had to take at the last budget, including national insurance chosen. They still can't say whether they'd reverse them. They know nothing about the damage they did to our economy.

Can I thank her for raising these tragic cases which have a huge impact on families, friends and communities. And I know that she's a passionate and dedicated campaigner on this issue. Every single life that's lost to knife crime devastates communities, and that's why we've banned zombie knives and ninja swords and are strengthening controls on online knife sales. Mr. Speaker, we're also giving stronger powers for police in our Crime and Policing Bill, which both the Conservatives and Reform voted against.

Well, I'm grateful for him raising this and I think the broken SEND system is the issue that's been raised with me more frequently than any other issue at Prime Minister's Questions. That's why we do need to review it. It's not working for any of those involved, particularly children and parents. It is important that we get it right and in so far as we can that we get a consensus about how we go forward, and that's what we're attempting to do.

Well, Mr. Speaker, can I begin by paying tribute to her sister Margaret, who was a guiding figure in the Labour Party, and the powerful legacy that she left in helping us to tackle brain cancer. We are determined to improve cancer survival rates and hit all NHS waiting times in relation to cancer so no patient waits longer than they should. And that's why we're investing 1.5 billion pounds in new surgical hubs and diagnostic scanners to help deliver over 30,000 more procedures and over 1.2 million diagnostic tests.

Can I thank her for raising this and you'll have heard the answer I gave just a few moments ago. what I will ensure is that she gets a meeting with the relevant minister so she can put the case in relation to the banking hub in question.

Can I also welcome the Canadian speaker? And can I also welcome Mervyn Kersh to the gallery today? He's a member of our greatest generation, a D-Day veteran who entered Bergen-Belsen days after it was liberated. Mervyn is 100 years old. I'm lucky to have met him twice and I know that it took him many, many years before he felt he could even begin to tell his story. And we thank him for his service and the story that he has told us in respect of that. As we mark Armistice Day, we give our eternal thanks to Mervyn and all those who served and remember the extraordinary sacrifice of ordinary people who fought to defend our freedom. Mr. Speaker, the House will also want to join me in remembering Holocaust survivor, Manfred Goldberg. He showed the most extraordinary courage to share his testimony. And in his memory, we must ensure that never again means never again. Mr. Speaker, I welcome the news that SSE have announced that they will spend 33 billion pounds on clean energy projects in this country. That's a major vote of confidence in the UK economy, happening because of our decisions to embrace the opportunities of clean power. Mr. Speaker, this morning I had meetings with ministerial colleagues and others. In addition to my duties in this House, I shall have further such meetings later today.

Well, it's always great to hear from the successor for Kwasi Kwarteng's constituency, Mr. Speaker. I'm very proud to represent our country on the world stage last week in COP, before that in NATO, and it's because of the reputation we've rebuilt over the last 15, 16 months that other countries now want to do trade deals with us and want to place their orders with us.

Well, I know how committed she is to righting historic wrongs for our mining communities and I can assure her so am I. She will know we've already transferred 1.5 billion pounds that was wrongly kept from over 100,000 former mineworkers. Ministers as she knows have met the BCSSS trustees on several occasions, the industry minister is meeting them later on today and I'll make sure that she's updated in relation to that.

Mr. Speaker, my focus each and every day is on rebuilding and renewing our country. But let me be absolutely clear, any attack on any member of my cabinet is completely unacceptable. And the health secretary, Mr. Speaker, in relation to health secretary, he promised before the election that in the first year of a Labour government we'd deliver 2 million extra appointments. We didn't deliver 2 million or 3 or 4, we delivered 5 million extra appointments. And today the health secretary is in Manchester where he's announced that because of the action he's taken to abolish NHS England, he's putting more people on the front line. He's doing a great job as is the whole of my cabinet.

Morgan McSweeney, my team and I are absolutely focused on delivering for the country. And let me be clear, of course Mr. Speaker, I never authorize attacks on cabinet members. I appointed them to their posts because they're the best people to carry out their jobs. And Mr. Speaker, she asks about waiting lists, waiting lists are down under this government, the number of GPs is up and because we scrapped NHS England we're investing on the front line. That's what the health secretary is doing today, getting on with his job and he's doing a very good job too.

Mr. Speaker, this is a united team and we are delivering together. Look what we delivered: the fastest growth in the G7, five interest rate cuts, trade deals with the EU, the US and India, all of which they opposed, we've delivered. And I can update the House...

Mr. Speaker, I can update the House, the Bank of England has upgraded growth today, we've secured 230 billion pounds of private investment and just this morning, I thought she might welcome it, the SSE have announced 33 billion pounds of investment in clean power. That's what this team are delivering for the country, fixing the mess that they left.

Mr. Speaker, let me give the House the details. 329,000 people more are in work since the start of this year. So 329,000 more are in work. Of course I accept we need to do more in relation to unemployment, that's why we're transforming job centers which they oppose, that's why we're working with 60 major businesses to tackle ill health in the workplace and invested 3.8 billion pound in tailored back to work support which they oppose. I would also remind the leader of the opposition, Mr. Speaker, that the average unemployment in the 14 years of her government was 5.4%, higher than the rate today.

Mr. Speaker, I've told the leader of the opposition why we increased national insurance, it's because of the mess that they left the country in, the NHS on its knees. Now we've got 5 million extra appointments, waiting lists down and 2,500 more GPs as a result of our decisions. But it's nearly the one year anniversary, but she still hasn't told us in relation to national insurance whether she agrees and admits that we should do it or if not, if that's her position, how she would find the money that we raised in the budget. She's had a whole year to think about that question, perhaps now she can give us an answer.

Mr. Speaker, the stupid mistakes were made over 14 long years, they broke the economy and now they think that they can lecture us. And now they've got this un-serious idea that they can find 47 billion pounds of cuts without saying where they're going to come from. No wonder that's called flimsy. Meanwhile, we're rebuilding the country, wages up, investment up, mortgages down.

My sympathy is with the people of Kent whose lives are being disrupted by the staggering incompetence of Reform. Mr. Speaker, Kent County Council was supposed to be the blueprint for what Reform would deliver across the country. Now we can see what that means: cutting local services, raising council tax, failing to protect the public. That's all Reform have to offer: grievance, division and total incompetence.

Let me be clear, I believe in a strong and independent BBC. Some would rather the BBC didn't exist. Some of them are sitting up there. I'm not one of them. In an age of disinformation, the argument for impartial British news service is stronger than ever. And where mistakes are made, they do need to get their house in order and the BBC must uphold the highest standards, be accountable and correct errors quickly. But I will always stand up for a strong independent BBC.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly agree with the comment that the last government undermined the work of the BBC. They undermined pretty well everything they did in 14 years. Mr. Speaker, I'm not going to go into the individual runnings of the BBC. I am a strong supporter of the BBC in the terms I've already set out.

Well, Mr. Speaker, November marks the first ever care leavers month and that is a time to recognize that every child deserves support to achieve their potential. And through our landmark Children's Wellbeing Bill, we're requiring every local authority to help care leavers find and secure accommodation. It saddens me that the parties opposite voted against it. The comments about children in care being evil are utterly appalling. And now the member for Clacton has heard them, I'm sure he'll want to condemn them right now.

Mr. Speaker, we will grip the mess we inherited and close every hotel. At their peak, under the previous government, there were 400 hotels, now there are only 200 remaining. But he says he doesn't have time to condemn the comments calling children in care evil. He's also not had the time, it appears, to condemn the racist comments of his own MP. Utterly spineless.

Well, Mr. Speaker, I was very proud to attend COP last week and the UK is leading on tackling climate change, delivering energy security and getting bills down and generating hundreds of jobs across the country. We're investing over 250 million pounds to put rooftop solar on schools, hospitals and military sites across the country. And that will deliver 400 million pounds of savings to renew our public services.

Can I absolutely recognize the need to address the imbalance between electricity and gas prices. We are exploring options to create a fairer system and I'm happy for ministers to keep him updated on what we're looking at. It's thanks to those levies and Labour's expansion of the warm homes discount that 6 million families will be getting 150 pounds off their energy bills this winter. And I know that he will welcome the 33 billion in investment from SSE, helping connect clean energy to areas across Scotland where it's most needed.

Mr. Speaker, I'm appalled that we inherited such a situation where tooth decay is the most common reason where children between five and nine are admitted to hospital, every children's hospital under their watch. Going in five to nine, this was I was very shocked when I heard this the first time at Alder Hey Hospital up in the North West. That more children being admitted to have their teeth taken out because they're rotting between the ages of five to nine than any other operation. That was their record, they should just be ashamed of it, ashamed of it. It's why I'm determined to rebuild NHS dentistry. I can confirm that discussions are underway with the sector, including the British Dental Association on fundamental reform to the dental contract to get her constituents the care that they need and that they deserve.

Can I thank him for raising this really serious issue, which has been raised by others across these benches on previous occasions and is a very serious issue. It is simply not right that customers and staff have been so badly let down. The care minister has convened representatives from across the industry to resolve the situation as quickly as possible. And I want to reassure him that we're working speedily to consider how to strengthen regulation of these pharmacies and I'll update the House as soon as I can.

I'm pleased to tell him that 100 million pounds has now been passed to Hospice UK so places like Garden House in his constituency can create the best environment to deliver care. That's backed, Mr. Speaker, by 26 million pounds investment for children and young people's hospices. We're also investing over 3 million pounds in researching palliative and end-of-life care through the National Institute for Health and Care Research. We're working on further proposals to improve the access, quality and sustainability of care and I'll make sure that ministers keep him updated.

Well, the Supreme Court ruling must be implemented in full and at all levels, she's absolutely right about that. She's raised these examples with me, I will make sure they're looked into and make sure she gets a proper reply in relation to the particular examples.

Well, that's a very appealing invitation just at the moment, Mr. Speaker. I'm proud to be putting power and resources directly back in the hands of local people in communities like Rhyl. That 20 million pounds can be used for issues that matter most to them, including revitalizing their high street, a cause that I know is crucial to many residents including hers. Just one in 14 communities across Wales is benefiting from the pride in place funding. This is the renewal you get with a Labour government working with a Labour government in Cardiff.

Can I tell him that our starting point is that we must always make sure that every mother is heard, understood and gets the quality of care that is needed. The independent national maternity investigation and local health needs assessment are due to report in spring of next year as he says. It's right that the recommendations of both of them are closely considered in any decision for Cheltenham and I'll make sure that he's kept updated as that rolls out.

Well, as he knows my number one priority is growth, so I'm very glad to see his upper lip. He's obviously championing this himself. And can I send my best wishes to everyone growing a mustache this Movember. It is right, Mr. Speaker, to highlight that men are hit harder by a range of conditions including cancer, cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes. And that's why our men's health strategy will set out actions to improve the health of all men in England.

Can I first say that any attack is to be condemned and it is absolutely right and we're determined that there is a criminal justice response in relation to attacks however it's carried out and whoever it is carried out by. But reintroducing the death penalty is not the answer to this. It didn't work when it was in place, it led to the death of those that in fact were turned out were innocent. But what we must do is improve as we are the criminal justice response in this country.

One of the greatest honors in this role is meeting and thanking our armed forces for their service which obviously we've been able to do during the course of this weekend and this week. Our ambition is to bring the armed forces covenant fully into law in the next armed forces bill and we will do so. We're also renewing the contract with those who serve through our veteran strategy including homes for heroes, a new network of support centers connecting charities and services with veterans. And Labour patriots stand with all those who serve and have served our country.

Can I begin by thanking him for his service to our country. And when former service chiefs raise an issue, we will of course engage with them, of course I respect their service and their views and we'll do so. We are having to get rid of unlawful legislation and putting in place a system with clear rights and protections for veterans and we'll continue to try to get that balance right.

Well, can I commend her, she's been a long-standing campaigner on this important issue. And the public is right to be furious about how the last government allowed sewage to pour into our lakes, rivers and seas. Alongside tough new powers to combat pollution, this ban will put an end to plastic wet wipes that litter our beaches, clog up our sewers and harm wildlife.

Well, I'm grateful to him for raising that and I'll look at the particular example that he's raised. As he will know, we're rolling out hubs, some of them already in place and more to come and I'll happily update him on where they're likely to be.

Well, first my thoughts are with Lily and her family and the details he raises are really deeply concerning. I know he's raised this with health ministers and I'll make sure he gets a swift response. He is a powerful advocate for change and I share his determination that everyone with an eating disorder gets the care and the support that they need.

Mr Speaker, let me start by congratulating Scotland on their magnificent victory last night, qualifying for the World Cup for the first time since 1998. I didn't realize you were all Scottish MPs. Mr Speaker, they qualified with fantastic goals, including a cracker from former Arsenal player Kieran Tierney, who was always a favorite with the fans. Mr Speaker, my thoughts are with the communities across the country affected by severe flooding, particularly in Monmouthshire. I've been liaising with the First Minister of Wales, and I want to thank all our emergency services for their response. Mr Speaker, my thoughts are also with the family and loved ones of Royal Fleet Auxiliary member James Elliot, who has sadly been lost. I know the contribution that personnel of the Royal Fleet Auxiliary make and the risks that they take in the line of duty. My thoughts, and I'm sure the thoughts of the whole House, are with those who knew him at this tragic and difficult time for them. Mr Speaker, last Thursday I visited Anglesey to announce the construction of the country's first small modular reactor. That's the biggest investment in North Wales in a generation, creating more than 6,000 jobs. On Monday we introduced the largest overhaul of the asylum policy in modern times, restoring control, fairness and creating safe and legal routes. And today I'm pleased to announce that inflation is coming down. There's more to do, but it's an important step. Mr Speaker, this morning I had meetings with ministerial colleagues and others; in addition to my duties in this House, I shall have further such meetings later today.

Can I thank him for his question? I know he feels strongly about this issue. As he says, the government is neutral on the passage of the bill. It is a matter of conscience, and there are different and respected views across Parliament, and it is for Parliament to decide in the end on any changes in this Chamber. Scrutiny of the bill in the Lords is a matter for the Lords, but the government does have a responsibility to make sure that any legislation which passes through Parliament is workable, is effective, and of course enforceable.

Well, well can I thank him for raising this important issue? Because they laugh, but working people paid a very heavy price for 14 years of economic failure. Austerity damaged the economy and decimated public services. A botched Brexit deal stifled growth, and the reckless borrowing of the mini-budget saw mortgages and the cost of living soar. He's right to raise this issue; we're determined to tackle inequality. He'll be pleased to know that under this government, wages are up, but we need to do more. We've had a pay increase for the 3.5 million lowest paid, and the Chancellor will deliver a budget based on labor values.

Well, well I'll inform her the budget's actually next week rather than after the budget; still got one week to go. But I can tell her it'll be a labor budget, Mr Speaker, with labor values. That means we will concentrate on cutting NHS waiting lists, cutting debt, and cutting the cost of living. And because of the decisions we've already made, inflation is down this morning. The Bank of England have upgraded growth. We've got a record 230 billion pounds of investment into this country under this government.

Mr Speaker, the budget is one week today and we will lay out our plans. But what we won't do, Mr Speaker, I've said what we will do in terms of protecting the NHS and public services. What we won't do is inflict austerity on the country as they did for 14 years. What we won't do is inflict a borrowing spree like Liz Truss did, which also inflicted huge damage. And Mr Speaker, have they learned anything? She's apparently got a golden economic rule, I think, it's a very important rule, this golden rule that she's set, this 47 billion pounds of cuts with no detail. No wonder the Institute of Government says they're on very shaky foundations. They haven't listened and they haven't learned.

Mr Speaker, every week she comes along and speculates and distorts. Last year, Mr Speaker, last year they predicted recession. And what did we get? The fastest growing economy in the G7 in the first half of the year. They opposed NHS investment and what did we get? Five million extra appointments in the first year of a Labour government. They tried growing the economy with millions on NHS waiting lists, with our schools crumbling and holes in our roads. It didn't work. What do they want to do now? Go back to the same failed experiment.

Mr Speaker, she talks about inflation; it went to 11% on them. 11% and the country is still paying the price. Inflation is down this morning, wages are up, and we've had five interest rate cuts, and that's because our fiscal rules are ironclad. And the Leader of the Opposition and the party opposite have no credibility on the economy. She was Treasury Minister during the worst decline in living standards on record. And she said that Liz Truss got the mini-budget 100% right. Not much room for flexibility there, 100% - that's pretty full marks, Mr Speaker. She might want to tell us if that's still her position: 100% right for Liz Truss.

Mr Speaker, let let me just say about ExxonMobil, it is a difficult time for the workforce there and we must focus on supporting them. We've been meeting with the company for over six months and explored every possible reasonable avenue. They have been facing losses for the last five years; it's best to do the detail before you chunter. And they're currently losing 1 million pounds a week. But she talks about policy and approach. On energy policy, she follows Reform. On the European Convention, she follows the man who wants her job. And when her Shadow Minister said we should deport people lawfully here to achieve "cultural coherence", she pretended that it didn't happen. I could go on; she was the Trade Secretary that didn't sign any trade deals. Cheerleader for the mini-budget, cheerleader for open borders. And when they were crashing the economy, botching Brexit, and running down the NHS, she was right at the center. She hasn't got an ounce of credibility.

Mr Speaker, either we renew our country with Labour or we go back to austerity 2.0 with Reform and the Tories. They left waiting lists at record highs, almost a million more children in poverty, and they wrecked our public services. She comes here to talk down the country; we're turning the page. More NHS appointments, free breakfast clubs, free childcare, more homes and better public services. That's what we're fighting for: a Britain built for all.

Well, my honorable friend is a brilliant champion for South Dorset and he's right to champion revitalizing our high streets. The Minister for Heritage would be delighted to discuss how we can get this iconic building reopened as he wants. I'm pleased that Weymouth secured 20 million pounds in pride in place funding, giving his community the power and resources to make a real difference to people's lives.

Can I join him on wishing Wales well, and Northern Ireland? I'd like to see all four nations in the finals. But look, he raises the really important issue of suicide and it's Mental Health Day and it is really important and I think the whole House would want to work together on anything that can prevent suicide. I think it'll all of us think about individuals we may know who lost their lives through suicide. It's something that touches almost every one of us and all of our families as well. We will of course look at the link between suicide and gambling and take whatever measures we can to reduce suicide. It's a very important issue.

Firstly, these are utterly appalling scenes. Utterly appalling. A criminal investigation, as you know, is underway, and specialist officers are tracking down those responsible. The Environmental Agency, in answer to his question, will use all available powers to make sure that the perpetrators cover the cost of the cleanup which must now follow. We have boosted the Environment Agency's budget for tackling waste crime by 50%, given councils new powers to seize and crush fly-tippers' vehicles, and lawbreakers can now face up to five years in jail.

I'm proud, Mr Speaker, to lead an open, tolerant, generous country. To maintain that principle, we must restore order and control, fix the utterly broken system left by the party opposite, and end the division that others seek to exploit. Lance Corporal Hooley was injured in a tragic accident away from the front lines while observing Ukrainian forces testing a new defensive capability. His life was full of courage and determination. He served our country with honor and distinction around the world in the cause of freedom and democracy, including as part of the small number of British personnel in Ukraine. Mr. Speaker, I place his name on record today to express our gratitude and respect and to affirm that his service will never be forgotten. Mr. Speaker, on Monday I hosted President Zelenskyy, President Macron, and Chancellor Scholz in Downing Street. We must redouble our efforts. The UK, Europe, and our allies will stand shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine, stand up to Putin's aggression, and work to deliver a just and lasting peace. Mr. Speaker, this morning I had meetings with ministerial colleagues and others. In addition to my duties in this house, I shall have further such meetings later today.

Well, can I say this country will always be compassionate in relation to refugees and comply with our full obligations under the various conventions. It is important that we address some of the challenges we face at the moment, but we mustn't lose sight that we've always been a compassionate country that welcomes refugees to our shores.

Can I thank her for raising this? And I'm proud that babies born today will have a better start in life thanks to our decisions. It is a moral mission of this government to lift children out of poverty and we intend to do so. Mr. Speaker, my own MPs are very proud we've just passed a budget which protected our public services and our NHS. No austerity which brought our NHS to the ground. We've created the conditions for economic stability with the headroom we need. And Mr. Speaker, we're concentrating on the single most important issue for families up and down the country, which is the cost of living, by taking 150 pounds off their energy bills. Mr. Speaker, I'm very pleased to say we're taking 150 pounds off energy bills. Prime Minister. Mr. Speaker, last week I pointed out that three of her ex-MPs went to Reform. That included the former deputy chairman Jonathan Gullis. More than when they left office. I'm very proud to say so. We're on an upward trajectory. And Mr. Speaker, Mr. Speaker, they left, they left our health service on its knees. 3,000 more by the end of March and we're rising on police numbers. Mr. Speaker, they left, they left the Home Office, the criminal justice system is utterly broken. Mr. Speaker, they left the NHS in an absolute mess, an absolute mess. With the highest waiting lists on record and the lowest confidence in the NHS ever. What did they do? Having broken it, they voted against that investment. They should hang their heads in shame.

Mr. Speaker, she's living proof you can say whatever you like when nobody is listening to anything you have to say. Absolutely no substance. She's no credibility on the economy. On issue after issue, she's clinging on to Reform. That's not leadership. It's weakness. No wonder so many are leaving her party. They know there's absolutely no reason to stay. Ed Davey.

Well, I thank him for raising this serious issue for his constituent and constituents and over 1.7 million homeowners across the country who are left at the mercy of unfair costs and poor management. That's a vital part of our leasehold reforms to protect homeowners from high costs and make sure everyone has the amenities that they need. Ed Davey, Leader of the Liberal Democrats.

Can I join him in congratulating Lando for the incredible win? On the question of Europe and President Trump's comments, what I see is a strong Europe united behind Ukraine and united behind our longstanding values of freedom and democracy, and I will always stand up for those values and those freedoms. Ed Davey.

Well, Mr. Speaker, we have got a close relationship with the EU through our reset earlier this year. And yes, I do want a closer relationship than the one we've got at the moment. We're moving towards that. We do have manifesto commitments on issues such as single market, customs union, and freedom of movement. But I would gently point this out, that having now done significant trade deals with other countries, including the US and India, which are hugely important to the JLR workforce and on pharma, it is not now sensible to unravel what is effectively the best deal with the US that any country has got.

Mr. Speaker is right, waiting lists are falling with over 5 million extra appointments. More people are being seen within 18 weeks, and we've hired 2,600 new GPs. That's real progress thanks to the hard work of NHS staff, backed by our record investment. I do think the strikes are unjustified and they threaten that hard-won progress, and the focus should always be on patients.

Mr. Speaker, I went to Solihull to see the JLR workforce before we got the deal with President Trump. They were worried sick that they were going to lose their jobs and that would be a loss for them, their families, and their communities. I took the call from President Trump when we got the deal in Solihull in JLR so the first people I could tell were the workforce who knew very well that that meant their jobs were safeguarded. We've also just done a deal on pharma, which is the first of its kind in the world and the best of its kind in the world. It is not sensible or fair to the JLR workforce or to the pharma sector to say having achieved those things now, we should unravel them by discussion about a customs union. I just don't think it's a sensible way to take our country forward. Josh Simons.

Well, I thank him for his question. The party opposite presided over a lost decade for our young people. I'm determined to support every young person to reach their potential. That's why we're delivering the first national youth strategy for 15 years to transform youth services backed by over 500 million pounds. Mr. Speaker, that means more youth workers, more youth centers, and a network of 50 Young Future Hubs. That's on top of our youth job guarantee and our plan to create 50,000 more apprenticeships. We're building a Britain for the next generation. Zaqir Matin.

Well, Mr. Speaker, we do support our churches and the work that those within our churches do, particularly in the lead up to Christmas, and I've got a reception for them in Downing Street this very afternoon. Jim Dickson.

Mr. Speaker, welfare ballooned on their watch. When the Shadow Chancellor was responsible for welfare, it ballooned by 33 billion pounds. They left a 22 billion pound black hole. The OBR reviewed and said they added 16 billion to that. We'll take no lecture from them on the economy. Final question, Karl Turner.

Well, he's absolutely right to draw attention to the crisis in our courts. Yes, he says. Sir Brian Leveson is one of our most respected senior judges. A system near total collapse, where victims of sexual violence and rape wait years to get justice. That is not justice. That is victims failed. Mr. Speaker, the anti-Semitic terror attack on Bondi Beach was sickening. It has had a profound impact around the world, including on Jewish communities here in the United Kingdom. Can I thank her and I know that Gazan students face huge challenges in taking up their places and we're considering solutions for those yet to arrive. Mr. Speaker, we continue to focus on aid into Gaza and I'll make sure my honorable friend is kept up to date on the next steps for students.

Mr. Speaker, I'm very proud that at the budget we had record investment into our public services. We stabilized the economy and we bore down on the cost of living. Well, can I thank him for raising this really important issue and it is really important that we have actions that match the words that we have expressed in response to these horrific attacks. The actions we've taken so far are increasing the funding for Jewish security up to 28 million pounds. I'm pleased to do that, but I'm sad to do that. Having to pay more money to provide security for people to be at their place of worship and to go to school is a sad thing for this country to have to do. I've ordered a review of protest and hate crime laws to stop protest breeding hatred. We're looking at new police powers to deal with repeat and targeted protests. And we've launched a review and training to tackle anti-Semitism in the NHS. There are other steps that we are talking to the community about taking, but all of those actions have already started.

Thank you.
